papers.conclusion: Only one of the evaluated SAEs reached the neuron baseline and none reached the DAS skyline, indicating current SAEs are not superior to neurons for this causal disentanglement task, but the evaluation is a useful step for assessing SAEs in interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Using representations reconstructed by SAEs degrades the model's knowledge of cities.
The end-to-end SAEs degrade knowledge less relative to their reconstruction loss, but this is weak evidence.
There is a significant gap between the neuron baseline and the DAS skyline, showing neurons can be improved upon.
Current SAEs for GPT-2 small generally perform below the neuron baseline, with only the top-k Open AI SAE matching it.
The top-k SAE (Open AI SAE) is the most performant among the evaluated SAEs.
papers.limitation: The evaluation is limited to GPT-2 small and a specific dataset (cities, countries, continents). Future work should scale to larger models and more attributes.
future_direction: Scale experiments to models with available SAEs including gemma, Mistral, Llama, and Pythia.
Use more attributes from the RA VEL dataset, such as language, gender, etc., for larger models with more knowledge.
papers.abstract: A popular new method in mechanistic interpretability is to train high-dimensional sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on neuron activations and use SAE features as the atomic units of analysis. However, the body of evidence on whether SAE feature spaces are useful for causal analysis is underdeveloped. In this work, we use the RAVEL benchmark to evaluate whether SAEs trained on hidden representations of GPT-2 small have sets of features that separately mediate knowledge of which country a city is in and which continent it is in. We evaluate four open-source SAEs for GPT-2 small against each other, with neurons serving as a baseline, and linear features learned via distributed alignment search (DAS) serving as a skyline. For each, we learn a binary mask to select features that will be patched to change the country of a city without changing the continent, or vice versa. Our results show that SAEs struggle to reach the neuron baseline, and none come close to the DAS skyline. We release code here: https://github.com/MaheepChaudhary/SAE-Ravel

papers.title: Don't Forget It! Conditional Sparse Autoencoder Clamping Works for Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders be used to unlearn harmful knowledge in large language models while retaining safe knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a conditional SAE-based clamping method for unlearning that improves retention of safe information compared to prior SAE methods and performs comparably to RMU with better interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning outperforms prior SAE approaches on retention and performs comparably with RMU on forgetting harmful information while retaining safe information, with fewer hyperparameters and better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal Clamp achieves the lowest WMDP-bio accuracy (0.2718) and highest alignment score (0.8226), indicating effective unlearning with some impact on general knowledge.
Clamp Prime improves forgetting performance (WMDP-bio accuracy drops to 0.2985) but slightly reduces general knowledge retention compared to RMU.
Adversarial evaluation using Concurrent Greedy Search shows that unlearned models resist suffix attacks, continuing to output gibberish.
The method requires fewer hyperparameter choices than RMU while maintaining interpretability.
SAE-based unlearning is shown to be viable, with conditional steering reducing side effects on safe information.
papers.limitation:
Training sparse autoencoders and labeling the latents is slow and expensive, limiting practicality to models with pre-existing SAEs.
Steering models with sparse autoencoders requires closed weights, as attackers can remove steering hooks if they have access to the weights.
Using Wikitext as the retain set for RMU may cause bias, potentially inflating the method's score on biology-related subjects in evaluation.
future_direction: Investigating which SAE layers allow for the best unlearning.
Exploring the impact of latent space dimensionality (i.e., using SAEs with larger hidden activation shapes).
Training interpretable parameters that edit the SAE latent vector to allow for fully interpretable fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in Large Language Model (LLM) capabilities have brought great potential but also posed new risks. For example, LLMs with knowledge of bioweapons, advanced chemistry, or cyberattacks could cause violence if placed in the wrong hands or during malfunctions. Because of their nature as near-black boxes, intuitive interpretation of LLM internals remains an open research question, preventing developers from easily controlling model behavior and capabilities. The use of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) has recently emerged as a potential method of unraveling representations of concepts in LLMs internals, and has allowed developers to steer model outputs by directly modifying the hidden activations. In this paper, we use SAEs to identify unwanted concepts from the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset within gemma-2-2b internals and use feature steering to reduce the model's ability to answer harmful questions while retaining its performance on harmless queries. Our results bring back optimism to the viability of SAE-based explicit knowledge unlearning techniques.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders to large language models and how should we evaluate their quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for scaling sparse autoencoders using a TopK activation function to directly control sparsity and techniques to prevent dead latents, establishes scaling laws, and proposes new metrics for evaluating feature quality.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can be scaled effectively with the proposed methods, and larger autoencoders yield better features according to the introduced evaluation metrics.
papers.key_findings:
TopK activation function improves the reconstruction-sparsity frontier and simplifies training compared to ReLU autoencoders with L1 penalty.
Techniques like tied initialization and an auxiliary loss reduce dead latents to 7% in a 16 million latent autoencoder.
Clean scaling laws are found with respect to autoencoder size and sparsity.
Larger autoencoders generally improve feature quality according to new metrics (probe loss, explainability, ablation sparsity).
The method scales to training a 16 million latent autoencoder on GPT-4 activations.
papers.limitation:
The probe-based evaluation metric leans on strong assumptions about what kinds of features are natural.
Evaluating explanation precision for arbitrary English explanations is computationally expensive.
future_direction: Explore ways to make it more tractable to approximate precision for arbitrary English explanations.
Scale to even larger autoencoders and apply the method to other models and modalities.
Improve evaluation metrics for feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising unsupervised approach for extracting interpretable features from a language model by reconstructing activations from a sparse bottleneck layer. Since language models learn many concepts, autoencoders need to be very large to recover all relevant features. However, studying the properties of autoencoder scaling is difficult due to the need to balance reconstruction and sparsity objectives and the presence of dead latents. We propose using k-sparse autoencoders [Makhzani and Frey, 2013] to directly control sparsity, simplifying tuning and improving the reconstruction-sparsity frontier. Additionally, we find modifications that result in few dead latents, even at the largest scales we tried. Using these techniques, we find clean scaling laws with respect to autoencoder size and sparsity. We also introduce several new metrics for evaluating feature quality based on the recovery of hypothesized features, the explainability of activation patterns, and the sparsity of downstream effects. These metrics all generally improve with autoencoder size. To demonstrate the scalability of our approach, we train a 16 million latent autoencoder on GPT-4 activations for 40 billion tokens. We release training code and autoencoders for open-source models, as well as a visualizer.

papers.title: Analysis of Variational Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE) and finds that it underperforms standard SAEs due to excessive KL divergence regularization causing feature death, disproving the hypothesis that variational methods improve feature organization.
papers.conclusion: The naive application of variational methods to sparse autoencoders does not improve feature organization or interpretability and is not a promising direction for SAE development.
papers.key_findings:
The vSAE underperforms the standard TopK SAE across core metrics like CE loss, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
The vSAE exhibits catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to KL divergence pressure pushing activations toward zero.
The vSAE shows improved performance on Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR) and Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) benchmarks, indicating more independent features.
t-SNE visualizations reveal that vSAE features are more dispersed and less clustered than SAE features, supporting the dispersive pressure hypothesis.
Despite having far fewer active features, the vSAE maintains feature interpretability, but the overall performance degradation suggests variational methods are not beneficial for SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The vSAE suffers from catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to excessive KL divergence regularization.
The observed improvements in feature independence (SCR, TPP) may be an artifact of the reduced dictionary size rather than principled organization.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach for interpreting neural network representations by learning sparse, human-interpretable features from dense activations. We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability. We introduce the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE), which replaces deterministic ReLU gating with stochastic sampling from learned Gaussian posteriors and incorporates KL divergence regularization toward a standard normal prior. Our hypothesis is that this probabilistic sampling creates dispersive pressure, causing features to organize more coherently in the latent space while avoiding overlap. We evaluate a TopK vSAE against a standard TopK SAE on Pythia-70M transformer residual stream activations using comprehensive benchmarks including SAE Bench, individual feature interpretability analysis, and global latent space visualization through t-SNE. The vSAE underperforms standard SAE across core evaluation metrics, though excels at feature independence and ablation metrics. The KL divergence term creates excessive regularization pressure that substantially reduces the fraction of living features, leading to observed performance degradation. While vSAE features demonstrate improved robustness, they exhibit many more dead features than baseline. Our findings suggest that naive application of variational methods to SAEs does not improve feature organization or interpretability.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) learn meaningful feature decompositions of neural network activations, or can their performance be matched by random baselines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) fail to reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms, as they recover very few ground-truth features in synthetic experiments and are matched in performance by simple random baselines on real model activations.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE evaluation practices are insufficient, and SAEs in their present state do not reliably learn meaningful feature decompositions. The proposed random baselines serve as simple sanity checks for future work.
papers.key_findings:
In synthetic experiments with known ground-truth features, SAEs recover only 9% of true features despite achieving 71% explained variance, showing a disconnect between reconstruction and feature recovery.
Three random baselines (Frozen Decoder, Soft-Frozen Decoder, Frozen Encoder) match fully-trained SAEs across key evaluation metrics: interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72).
In the synthetic variable probability setting, SAEs recover only the highest-frequency ground-truth features, leaving over 90% of the feature dictionary unmatched.
The reconstruction objective is a poor proxy for meaningful decomposition, as SAEs can achieve strong reconstruction without aligning with true features.
The competitive performance of frozen baselines suggests SAEs may operate in a 'lazy training' regime, achieving most gains through minimal adjustments to randomly initialized components.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic experiment assumes independent feature activations, omitting correlations that likely exist in real neural networks.
The work focuses on standard SAE architectures and does not evaluate related approaches such as transcoders or crosscoders.
future_direction: Explore objectives that more directly incentivize feature alignment rather than just reconstruction.
Design appropriate randomization baselines for related methods like transcoders and crosscoders.
Incorporate more realistic feature dependencies in synthetic evaluation setups.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for interpreting neural networks by decomposing their activations into sparse sets of human-interpretable features. Recent work has introduced multiple SAE variants and successfully scaled them to frontier models. Despite much excitement, a growing number of negative results in downstream tasks casts doubt on whether SAEs recover meaningful features. To directly investigate this, we perform two complementary evaluations. On a synthetic setup with known ground-truth features, we demonstrate that SAEs recover only $9\%$ of true features despite achieving $71\%$ explained variance, showing that they fail at their core task even when reconstruction is strong. To evaluate SAEs on real activations, we introduce three baselines that constrain SAE feature directions or their activation patterns to random values. Through extensive experiments across multiple SAE architectures, we show that our baselines match fully-trained SAEs in interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72). Together, these results suggest that SAEs in their current state do not reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: Evaluating Adversarial Robustness of Concept Representations in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of concept representations in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to adversarial input perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces robustness as a critical evaluation dimension for sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and demonstrates that SAE concept representations are vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations.
papers.conclusion: SAE interpretations are highly vulnerable to minimal input changes, raising concerns about their reliability in realistic settings, and motivating the development of more robust interpretability tools.
papers.key_findings:
Small adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate SAE concept representations without notably affecting the base LLM's activations.
SAE concept representations are not robust even to non-adversarial synonym replacements.
The attacks are effective across different models, datasets, and model depths.
Untargeted attacks are more successful at the population level, while targeted attacks are more effective at the individual level.
SAE latents that represent meaningful concepts are highly manipulable.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of attacks is bounded by compute constraints (single 80GB A100 GPU).
The choice of medium-sized LLMs results in slower attacks.
future_direction: Developing novel methods to denoise SAE activations and isolate reliable signals.
Extending the evaluation framework to other concept-extraction tools like transcoders and crosscoders.
Optimizing the attack pipeline to better balance effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly used to interpret the internal activations of large language models (LLMs) by mapping them to human-interpretable concept representations. While existing evaluations of SAEs focus on metrics such as the reconstruction-sparsity tradeoff, human (auto-)interpretability, and feature disentanglement, they overlook a critical aspect: the robustness of concept representations to input perturbations. We argue that robustness must be a fundamental consideration for concept representations, reflecting the fidelity of concept labeling. To this end, we formulate robustness quantification as input-space optimization problems and develop a comprehensive evaluation framework featuring realistic scenarios in which adversarial perturbations are crafted to manipulate SAE representations. Empirically, we find that tiny adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate concept-based interpretations in most scenarios without notably affecting the base LLM's activations. Overall, our results suggest that SAE concept representations are fragile and without further denoising or postprocessing they might be ill-suited for applications in model monitoring and oversight.

papers.title: Enhancing Neural Network Interpretability with Feature-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the feature learning of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to better align with input features, thereby enhancing their usefulness for neural network interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Mutual Feature Regularization (MFR), a regularization technique that trains multiple Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) in parallel with weight reinitialization and an auxiliary penalty to encourage learning similar features, leading to better alignment with input features and improved SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: MFR encourages SAEs to learn more features of the input, thereby increasing their usefulness for neural network interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MFR increases the correlation between feature similarity across SAEs and similarity with input features, as demonstrated on synthetic data.
On synthetic data, SAEs trained with MFR recover more of the known input features compared to baseline SAEs.
MFR improves reconstruction loss and loss recovered when training SAEs on GPT-2 Small MLP layer activations, with up to a 21.21% reduction in reconstruction loss.
MFR also improves reconstruction loss on EEG denoising tasks, though the benefits are smaller than for neural network activations.
The method involves conditionally reinitializing SAE weights based on inactive feature detection and adding an auxiliary penalty to encourage feature similarity across SAEs.
papers.limitation: MFR increases computational cost as it requires training multiple SAEs in parallel, which may become unmanageable for very large models.
future_direction: Investigate efficient mutual learning-based approaches for SAEs that can benefit from the positive relationship between feature similarity across SAEs and feature similarity with input features without requiring more compute.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in improving the interpretability of neural network activations, but can learn features that are not features of the input, limiting their effectiveness. We propose \textsc{Mutual Feature Regularization} \textbf{(MFR)}, a regularization technique for improving feature learning by encouraging SAEs trained in parallel to learn similar features. We motivate \textsc{MFR} by showing that features learned by multiple SAEs are more likely to correlate with features of the input. By training on synthetic data with known features of the input, we show that \textsc{MFR} can help SAEs learn those features, as we can directly compare the features learned by the SAE with the input features for the synthetic data. We then scale \textsc{MFR} to SAEs that are trained to denoise electroencephalography (EEG) data and SAEs that are trained to reconstruct GPT-2 Small activations. We show that \textsc{MFR} can improve the reconstruction loss of SAEs by up to 21.21\% on GPT-2 Small, and 6.67\% on EEG data. Our results suggest that the similarity between features learned by different SAEs can be leveraged to improve SAE training, thereby enhancing performance and the usefulness of SAEs for model interpretability.

papers.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Why do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) underperform relative to other techniques, and can we fix the problems? Specifically, the paper investigates the problem of 'feature hedging' in narrow SAEs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'feature hedging' as a fundamental problem in narrow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) where correlated features are merged, degrading monosemanticity, and proposes an improved variant called balance matryoshka SAEs to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Feature hedging is a core theoretical problem in SAEs that contributes to their underperformance, and the proposed balance matryoshka SAE architecture is a step towards addressing both hedging and absorption, though both problems remain.
papers.key_findings:
Feature hedging occurs when an SAE is too narrow to represent all underlying features and features are correlated, causing the SAE to merge components of correlated features into single latents.
Hedging is caused by the reconstruction (MSE) loss and becomes more severe the narrower the SAE.
In LLM SAEs, hedging is likely the norm due to the high number of correlated features and the SAE being narrower than the number of underlying features.
Balance matryoshka SAEs, which tune the relative loss coefficients between inner and outer levels, can improve performance by better balancing the competing forces of hedging and absorption.
SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging, while wider SAEs suffer more from absorption.
papers.limitation: Only test hedging in SAEs up to 65k latents on LLMs with 2b parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Improving balance matryoshka SAEs by learning different balancing coefficients per latent rather than a single coefficient for all latents.
papers.abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Which Sparse Autoencoder Features Are Real? Model-X Knockoffs for False Discovery Rate Control
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish real computational patterns from erroneous correlations in sparse autoencoder features? The paper investigates using Model-X knockoffs for false discovery rate control in SAE feature selection.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-X knockoffs for selecting sparse autoencoder features with false discovery rate control, revealing that only 25% of highly active SAE features encode genuine task-relevant information.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a rigorous statistical framework for identifying genuine SAE features with FDR control, addressing a critical gap in interpretability research and showing that naive feature analysis approaches are dominated by false positives.
papers.key_findings:
The method selected 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 from 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification.
Selected features show a 5.40× separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features.
Only about 25% of the examined latents carry task-relevant signal, while 75% do not.
A classifier using only the selected features achieved 77.4% training accuracy.
Features with negative knockoff statistics exist, indicating misleading patterns that would be selected by naive correlation-based approaches.
papers.limitation:
Feature reduction is necessary for stable covariance estimation (n > p), which may miss rare but important features.
Computational cost scales quadratically in p, becoming expensive for very large feature sets.
The method identifies which features are real but does not explain what those features represent.
The method identifies statistical association, not necessarily causal importance.
future_direction: Explore hierarchical testing strategies, approximate knockoff methods, or alternative covariance estimation techniques to handle p ≫ n settings.
Combine knockoff-based selection with automated interpretation pipelines to provide both statistical validation and conceptual understanding.
Investigate how feature validity varies across layers and tasks, and how selection interacts with different SAE training objectives and architectures.
papers.abstract: Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are crucial for identifying interpretable features in neural networks, it is still challenging to distinguish between real computational patterns and erroneous correlations. We introduce Model-X knockoffs to SAE feature selection, using knock-off+ to control the false discovery rate (FDR) with finite-sample guarantees under the standard Model-X assumptions (in our case, via a Gaussian surrogate for the latent distribution). We select 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 after analyzing 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification using Pythia-70M. About 25% of the latents under examination carry task-relevant signal, whereas 75% do not, according to the chosen set, which displays a 5.40x separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features. Our method offers a re-producible and principled framework for reliable feature discovery by combining SAEs with multiple-testing-aware inference, advancing the foundations of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Unveiling Language-Specific Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to identify and analyze language-specific features in multilingual Large Language Models, and what is the impact of these features on model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify language-specific features in LLMs and demonstrates that these features can be used to enhance steering vectors for better control over the language generated by the models.
papers.conclusion: The study uses SAEs to analyze multilingual capabilities in LLMs, identifying language-specific features that play a crucial role in language generation and can be leveraged to enhance steering vectors for improved language control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can exhibit strong monolingual characteristics, as measured by a novel monolinguality metric.
Language-specific features are not only tied to language-specific tokens but also to the language-specific linguistic context, as shown in code-switching experiments.
Ablating language-specific features via directional ablation significantly reduces model performance only in the target language, leaving other languages largely unaffected.
Some languages have multiple synergistic features; ablating them together yields a greater performance impact than ablating them individually.
Using language-specific features as gating signals to improve steering vectors achieves better control over the language generated by LLMs, with improved performance and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The method does not yet cover certain low-resource languages.
The SAE-based steering vectors sometimes underperform compared to the original steering vectors.
The SAEs used were not trained on curated multilingual data.
future_direction: Utilize language-specific features to guide the training process of multilingual language models.
Investigate low-resource languages to enhance the analysis.
Explore more refined approaches to improve the performance of SAE-based steering vectors.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms behind multilingual capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) have been examined using neuron-based or internal-activation-based methods. However, these methods often face challenges such as superposition and layer-wise activation variance, which limit their reliability. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offer a more nuanced analysis by decomposing the activations of LLMs into a sparse linear combination of SAE features. We introduce a novel metric to assess the monolinguality of features obtained from SAEs, discovering that some features are strongly related to specific languages. Additionally, we show that ablating these SAE features only significantly reduces abilities in one language of LLMs, leaving others almost unaffected. Interestingly, we find some languages have multiple synergistic SAE features, and ablating them together yields greater improvement than ablating individually. Moreover, we leverage these SAE-derived language-specific features to enhance steering vectors, achieving control over the language generated by LLMs. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aatrox103/multilingual-llm-features.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Denoising Concept Vectors with Sparse Autoencoders for Improved Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of linear concept vectors for language model steering by denoising hidden representations using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SDCV, a method that uses sparse autoencoders to denoise hidden representations by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples, leading to improved steering success rates.
papers.conclusion: SDCV effectively mitigates noise in concept vectors and enhances steering performance, demonstrating that denoising representations is a promising direction for robust concept steering.
papers.key_findings:
SDCV improves steering success rates by 4-16% across six challenging concepts while maintaining topic relevance.
SDCV-enhanced difference-in-mean generally outperforms SDCV-enhanced linear probing.
The method is effective across different models (Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B).
Optimal values for top-k and scale factor are not linearly related to peak performance, likely due to superposition and SAE training objectives.
Counterfactual experiments show that amplifying non-top-k latents (noise) generally decreases steering success.
papers.limitation:
The approach is confined to model families for which SAEs have already been trained.
SAEs imperfectly disentangle features and struggle to accurately capture feature importance.
Optimal values for steering strength, k, and scale factor must be determined empirically, which is computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: Linear concept vectors effectively steer LLMs, but existing methods suffer from noisy features in diverse datasets that undermine steering robustness. We propose Sparse Autoencoder-Denoised Concept Vectors (SDCV), which selectively keep the most discriminative SAE latents while reconstructing hidden representations. Our key insight is that concept-relevant signals can be explicitly separated from dataset noise by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples. Applied to linear probing and difference-in-mean, SDCV consistently improves steering success rates by 4-16\% across six challenging concepts, while maintaining topic relevance.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Code Correctness in LLMs via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally represent and process code correctness? The paper applies sparse autoencoders to identify and analyze directions in model representations that correspond to code correctness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses sparse autoencoders to identify and analyze code correctness directions in LLMs, revealing that error detection is reliable but correction via steering involves tradeoffs, and that these mechanisms persist from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify code correctness directions in LLMs, revealing mechanistic insights that have practical applications for prompting and error detection.
papers.key_findings:
Detection directions predict errors reliably (F1: 0.821) but fail as confidence indicators for correct code (F1: 0.504).
Steering interventions produce significant corrections but introduce tradeoffs, fixing 4.04% of errors but corrupting 14.66% of correct code.
Attention analysis shows test cases matter more than problem descriptions for successful code generation.
Weight orthogonalization proves correct directions are necessary for generation, their removal causing 83.62% corruption.
Code correctness features persist from base to chat models, with directions from base Gemma-2 retaining effectiveness after instruction-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The correct-predicting feature has low precision (0.362) due to false positives, limiting its utility as a confidence indicator.
Steering interventions correct only 4.04% of errors while corrupting 14.66% of correct code, indicating a tradeoff.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models become integral to software development, with substantial portions of AI-suggested code entering production, understanding their internal correctness mechanisms becomes critical for safe deployment. We apply sparse autoencoders to decompose LLM representations, identifying directions that correspond to code correctness. We select predictor directions using t-statistics and steering directions through separation scores from base model representations, then analyze their mechanistic properties through steering, attention analysis, and weight orthogonalization. We find that code correctness directions in LLMs reliably predict incorrect code, while correction capabilities, though statistically significant, involve tradeoffs between fixing errors and preserving correct code. Mechanistically, successful code generation depends on attending to test cases rather than problem descriptions. Moreover, directions identified in base models retain their effectiveness after instruction-tuning, suggesting code correctness mechanisms learned during pre-training are repurposed during fine-tuning. Our mechanistic insights suggest three practical applications: prompting strategies should prioritize test examples over elaborate problem descriptions, predictor directions can serve as error alarms for developer review, and these same predictors can guide selective steering, intervening only when errors are anticipated to prevent the code corruption from constant steering.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: GPCR-BERT: Interpreting Sequential Design of G Protein Coupled Receptors Using Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the correlation between variations in conserved motifs of GPCRs and other amino acids? Can we predict missing residues and identify key contributing amino acids?
papers.core_contribution: Developed GPCR-BERT, a fine-tuned protein language model, to interpret sequential design of GPCRs, achieving high accuracy in predicting masked residues and identifying residue correlations through attention analysis.
papers.conclusion: GPCR-BERT effectively predicts residues and distinguishes GPCR classes, providing insights into functional relationships and potential applications in mutation studies and drug development.
papers.key_findings:
GPCR-BERT achieved high accuracy (up to 100%) in predicting masked residues in conserved motifs.
The model successfully clustered GPCRs of the same class in embedding space, indicating it captures class-specific features.
Attention analysis revealed correlations between masked residues and other amino acids, some of which align with experimental mutagenesis data.
The model's predictions for CWxP motif were less accurate, likely due to smaller dataset size.
GPCR-BERT outperformed BERT and SVM on the prediction tasks, demonstrating the advantage of protein-specific pre-training.
papers.limitation: The conserved motifs are not 100% conserved (e.g., CWxP motif is only 71% conserved), so the model might not apply to GPCRs with varied versions of the motifs.
papers.abstract: With the rise of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs) in Chemistry and Biology, new avenues for the design and understanding of therapeutics have opened up to the scientific community. Protein sequences can be modeled as language and can take advantage of recent advances in LLMs, specifically with the abundance of our access to the protein sequence datasets. In this paper, we developed the GPCR-BERT model for understanding the sequential design of G Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are the target of over one-third of FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. However, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the relationship between amino acid sequence, ligand selectivity, and conformational motifs (such as NPxxY, CWxP, E/DRY). By utilizing the pre-trained protein model (Prot-Bert) and fine-tuning with prediction tasks of variations in the motifs, we were able to shed light on several relationships between residues in the binding pocket and some of the conserved motifs. To achieve this, we took advantage of attention weights, and hidden states of the model that are interpreted to extract the extent of contributions of amino acids in dictating the type of masked ones. The fine-tuned models demonstrated high accuracy in predicting hidden residues within the motifs. In addition, the analysis of embedding was performed over 3D structures to elucidate the higher-order interactions within the conformations of the receptors.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: A Survey on Sparse Autoencoders: Interpreting the Internal Mechanisms of Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models. It covers technical frameworks, explanation methods, evaluation metrics, and applications.
papers.limitation:
Incomplete Concept Dictionary
Lack Theoretical Foundations
Reconstruction Errors
Computational Burden
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. Recently, mechanistic interpretability has attracted significant attention from the research community as a means to understand the inner workings of LLMs. Among various mechanistic interpretability approaches, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method due to their ability to disentangle the complex, superimposed features within LLMs into more interpretable components. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of SAEs for interpreting and understanding the internal workings of LLMs. Our major contributions include: (1) exploring the technical framework of SAEs, covering basic architecture, design improvements, and effective training strategies; (2) examining different approaches to explaining SAE features, categorized into input-based and output-based explanation methods; (3) discussing evaluation methods for assessing SAE performance, covering both structural and functional metrics; and (4) investigating real-world applications of SAEs in understanding and manipulating LLM behaviors.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can find a canonical set of units of analysis (unique, complete, and atomic features) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis because smaller SAEs are incomplete (missing information) and larger SAEs learn composed, non-atomic features. The choice of SAE dictionary size should be pragmatic.
papers.conclusion: Alternative methods are required for identifying canonical units of analysis, and SAE practitioners should adopt a pragmatic approach to choosing dictionary size for interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE stitching reveals that larger SAEs contain novel latents that improve reconstruction when added to smaller SAEs, indicating smaller SAEs are incomplete.
SAE stitching shows that larger SAEs also contain reconstruction latents similar to those in smaller SAEs, but sometimes composed of multiple smaller latents.
Meta-SAEs can decompose larger SAE latents into interpretable meta-latents, demonstrating that larger SAE latents are not atomic.
Meta-latents are similar to latents found in smaller SAEs, suggesting larger SAE latents are compositions of smaller SAE latents.
The sparsity penalty in SAEs incentivizes the learning of composed features in larger dictionaries, rather than atomic features.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines two language models (GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B) and does not include very large SAEs.
Associating SAE latents with interpretable concepts remains an open problem, and the methods do not identify canonical units nor the optimal dictionary size.
future_direction: Pursue different approaches for identifying canonical units of analysis.
Pragmatically choose SAE dictionary size based on the specific interpretability task.
papers.abstract: A common goal of mechanistic interpretability is to decompose the activations of neural networks into features: interpretable properties of the input computed by the model. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for finding these features in LLMs, and it has been postulated that they can be used to find a \textit{canonical} set of units: a unique and complete list of atomic features. We cast doubt on this belief using two novel techniques: SAE stitching to show they are incomplete, and meta-SAEs to show they are not atomic. SAE stitching involves inserting or swapping latents from a larger SAE into a smaller one. Latents from the larger SAE can be divided into two categories: \emph{novel latents}, which improve performance when added to the smaller SAE, indicating they capture novel information, and \emph{reconstruction latents}, which can replace corresponding latents in the smaller SAE that have similar behavior. The existence of novel features indicates incompleteness of smaller SAEs. Using meta-SAEs -- SAEs trained on the decoder matrix of another SAE -- we find that latents in SAEs often decompose into combinations of latents from a smaller SAE, showing that larger SAE latents are not atomic. The resulting decompositions are often interpretable; e.g. a latent representing ``Einstein'' decomposes into ``scientist'', ``Germany'', and ``famous person''. Even if SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis, they may still be useful tools. We suggest that future research should either pursue different approaches for identifying such units, or pragmatically choose the SAE size suited to their task. We provide an interactive dashboard to explore meta-SAEs: https://metasaes.streamlit.app/

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scalably train Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on large language models, and how do these SAEs perform in terms of sparsity-fidelity trade-off, interpretability, and generalization to longer contexts and fine-tuned models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Llama Scope, a suite of 256 Sparse Autoencoders trained on every layer and sublayer of Llama-3.1-8B-Base, along with modifications to Top-K SAEs and a scalable training infrastructure, providing a resource for mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Llama Scope provides a comprehensive set of SAEs that advance the Pareto frontier of sparsity and reconstruction fidelity, and the SAEs generalize effectively to out-of-distribution settings, facilitating future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs outperform vanilla SAEs in sparsity-fidelity trade-off.
Wider SAEs (with more features) achieve better reconstruction quality at the same sparsity level.
SAEs trained on base models generalize well to longer contexts and instruction-finetuned models.
Feature geometry analysis confirms that feature splitting enables the discovery of new features.
The firing frequency distribution of SAE features is consistent with expected sparsity constraints.
papers.limitation:
The monosemanticity evaluation focuses on top activations and may not capture behavior on low-activating samples.
The online activation generation method can lead to redundant computation when training multiple SAEs on the same position.
future_direction: Exploring SAE-based circuit analysis and fine-grained causal analysis.
Conducting automated prompt-based evaluations across a wide range of tasks.
Fine-tuning SAEs for long-context data.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful unsupervised method for extracting sparse representations from language models, yet scalable training remains a significant challenge. We introduce a suite of 256 SAEs, trained on each layer and sublayer of the Llama-3.1-8B-Base model, with 32K and 128K features. Modifications to a state-of-the-art SAE variant, Top-K SAEs, are evaluated across multiple dimensions. In particular, we assess the generalizability of SAEs trained on base models to longer contexts and fine-tuned models. Additionally, we analyze the geometry of learned SAE latents, confirming that \emph{feature splitting} enables the discovery of new features. The Llama Scope SAE checkpoints are publicly available at~\url{https://huggingface.co/fnlp/Llama-Scope}, alongside our scalable training, interpretation, and visualization tools at \url{https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Language-Model-SAEs}.
