These contributions aim to advance the open-source Sparse Autoencoder ecosystem and support mechanistic interpretability research by reducing the need for redundant SAE training.

papers.title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: Applying sparse autoencoders to unlearn knowledge in language models
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models in an interpretable way.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that individual interpretable SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models, but current SAE quality or intervention techniques result in similar or larger side-effects than fine-tuning based methods like Representation Misdirection for Unlearning (RMU).
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning is possible but currently has limitations; improvements in SAE quality or intervention techniques are needed to make it comparable to fine-tuning based techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models.
Negative scaling of feature activations is necessary for unlearning; zero ablating features is ineffective.
Intervening on multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
The specific decoder vectors are important for unlearning in gemma-2-2b-it, but not as critical in gemma-2b-it.
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, not the weights, so the original knowledge remains in the weights.
papers.limitation:
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, without modifying the model weights, so the original knowledge is still contained in the weights.
Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.
SAE-based unlearning results in similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
future_direction: Examine how SAE quality and width impact unlearning effectiveness.
Compare SAE-based unlearning to activation steering using bio-related and non-bio-related prompt pairs.
Investigate how SAE interventions affect related features in subsequent layers to better understand the unlearning mechanism.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models. We use the biology subset of the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy dataset and test on the gemma-2b-it and gemma-2-2b-it language models. We demonstrate that individual interpretable biology-related SAE features can be used to unlearn a subset of WMDP-Bio questions with minimal side-effects in domains other than biology. Our results suggest that negative scaling of feature activations is necessary and that zero ablating features is ineffective. We find that intervening using multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple different topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing Representation Misdirection for Unlearning technique. Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.

papers.title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control large language model behavior in open-ended generation settings by using supervised steering in sparse, interpretable representation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised steering framework (SAE-SSV) that constrains interventions to a sparse, task-relevant latent subspace identified via labeled data and sparse autoencoders, enabling more targeted control and better preservation of generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SAE-SSV enables effective LLM steering by operating in sparse, task-specific subspaces, outperforming existing methods and providing a more targeted and interpretable approach to behavior control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-SSV consistently outperforms baseline steering methods (CAA, RePe, Top PC, ITI) in steering success rate across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity tasks.
A notably small subspace of SAE latent dimensions is sufficient for effective steering, enabling targeted and interpretable interventions.
Steering in the structured SAE subspace preserves or improves generation quality (lexical diversity, entropy) compared to baselines, which often degrade it.
The method generalizes to unseen datasets within the same task domain, capturing both semantic directions and stylistic patterns.
The top SAE features used for steering are interpretable and correspond to semantically meaningful concepts related to the target attribute.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which may not be available for all models or domains.
Only evaluated on LLMs with up to 9B parameters; scaling to larger models is future work.
Evaluation focused on open-ended generation tasks with limited human evaluation; generalizability to more specialized domains remains to be explored.
future_direction: Achieve universal and style-invariant SSVs that generalize across datasets, tasks, and model families by curating diverse training corpora and developing objectives that encourage semantic steering while minimizing stylistic sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, but controlling their behavior reliably remains challenging, especially in open-ended generation settings. This paper introduces a novel supervised steering approach that operates in sparse, interpretable representation spaces. We employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to obtain sparse latent representations that aim to disentangle semantic attributes from model activations. Then we train linear classifiers to identify a small subspace of task-relevant dimensions in latent representations. Finally, we learn supervised steering vectors constrained to this subspace, optimized to align with target behaviors. Experiments across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity steering tasks with multiple LLMs demonstrate that our supervised steering vectors achieve higher success rates with minimal degradation in generation quality compared to existing methods. Further analysis reveals that a notably small subspace is sufficient for effective steering, enabling more targeted and interpretable interventions. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Ineedanamehere/SAE-SSV.

papers.title: SAVE: Sparse Autoencoder-Driven Visual Information Enhancement for Mitigating Object Hallucination
papers.research_question: How can object hallucination in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be mitigated by using sparse autoencoders to identify and steer along visual understanding features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes SA VE, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to identify visual understanding features in MLLMs and steers the model along these features to mitigate object hallucination, outperforming training-free baselines.
papers.conclusion: SA VE effectively mitigates object hallucination in MLLMs by steering along visual understanding features identified via sparse autoencoders, demonstrating consistent improvements across models and benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can be used to identify visual understanding features that are discriminative between correct and hallucinated responses.
Steering along visual understanding features reduces object hallucination, while steering along hallucinated features amplifies it.
SA VE outperforms state-of-the-art training-free methods on CHAIR, POPE, and MMHal-Bench benchmarks.
Steering suppresses the probability of uncertain object tokens and increases attention to image tokens.
The method is robust across different MLLM architectures and layers.
papers.abstract: Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced substantially, they remain vulnerable to object hallucination caused by language priors and visual information loss. To address this, we propose SAVE (Sparse Autoencoder-Driven Visual Information Enhancement), a framework that mitigates hallucination by steering the model along Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) latent features. A binary object-presence question-answering probe identifies the SAE features most indicative of the model's visual information processing, referred to as visual understanding features. Steering the model along these identified features reinforces grounded visual understanding and effectively reduces hallucination. With its simple design, SAVE outperforms state-of-the-art training-free methods on standard benchmarks, achieving a 10\%p improvement in CHAIR\_S and consistent gains on POPE and MMHal-Bench. Extensive evaluations across multiple models and layers confirm the robustness and generalizability of our approach. Further analysis reveals that steering along visual understanding features suppresses the generation of uncertain object tokens and increases attention to image tokens, mitigating hallucination. Code is released at https://github.com/wiarae/SAVE.

papers.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) truly uncover all concepts a model relies on, or are they inherently biased toward certain kinds of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a duality framework between SAE architectures and concept geometry, showing that SAEs impose implicit assumptions about concept structure, and proposes a new SAE (SpaDE) that explicitly incorporates nonlinear separability and concept heterogeneity to recover previously hidden concepts.
papers.conclusion: There is no universal SAE architecture; the choice of SAE should be guided by the geometry of concepts in the model's representations, and data-aware design is essential for effective interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs are not universal; their architecture imposes implicit assumptions about concept structure (e.g., linear separability, uniform dimensionality) that bias what they can detect.
Existing SAEs (ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK) fail to recover concepts that are nonlinearly separable or have heterogeneous intrinsic dimensionality.
The proposed SpaDE SAE, which uses a sparsemax projection and Euclidean distances, can adaptively capture concepts with nonlinear separability and heterogeneous dimensionality.
Experiments on synthetic data, formal languages, and vision activations validate that SpaDE discovers concepts missed by other SAEs and maintains clearer concept boundaries.
The duality between SAE architecture and concept geometry suggests that interpretability tools must be designed with the data's concept structure in mind.
papers.limitation:
SpaDE assumes that Euclidean distances are meaningful in the concept space, which may not hold for all datasets.
The duality framework currently covers ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK, and SpaDE, but may not generalize to all SAE variants.
Experiments are limited to synthetic data, a formal language, and one vision dataset (Imagenette); broader validation is needed.
future_direction: Extend the duality framework to other SAE architectures and interpretability methods.
Automate the selection of SAE architecture based on data properties.
Explore more complex concept structures beyond nonlinear separability and heterogeneity.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret neural networks by identifying meaningful concepts from their representations. However, do SAEs truly uncover all concepts a model relies on, or are they inherently biased toward certain kinds of concepts? We introduce a unified framework that recasts SAEs as solutions to a bilevel optimization problem, revealing a fundamental challenge: each SAE imposes structural assumptions about how concepts are encoded in model representations, which in turn shapes what it can and cannot detect. This means different SAEs are not interchangeable -- switching architectures can expose entirely new concepts or obscure existing ones. To systematically probe this effect, we evaluate SAEs across a spectrum of settings: from controlled toy models that isolate key variables, to semi-synthetic experiments on real model activations and finally to large-scale, naturalistic datasets. Across this progression, we examine two fundamental properties that real-world concepts often exhibit: heterogeneity in intrinsic dimensionality (some concepts are inherently low-dimensional, others are not) and nonlinear separability. We show that SAEs fail to recover concepts when these properties are ignored, and we design a new SAE that explicitly incorporates both, enabling the discovery of previously hidden concepts and reinforcing our theoretical insights. Our findings challenge the idea of a universal SAE and underscores the need for architecture-specific choices in model interpretability. Overall, we argue an SAE does not just reveal concepts -- it determines what can be seen at all.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
papers.research_question: Do commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones?
papers.core_contribution: Common SAE metrics (e.g., auto-interpretability scores) do not reliably distinguish between trained and randomly initialized transformers, indicating these metrics are insufficient for validating interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: High aggregate auto-interpretability scores alone do not guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered; the paper recommends routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics similar to those from trained models.
Standard SAE quality metrics (explained variance, cosine similarity, L1 norm) show similar trends across trained and randomized variants.
Token distribution entropy reveals that features from randomized models remain simple and token-specific, unlike features from trained models which become more abstract across layers.
The area under the ROC curve (AUROC) for auto-interpretability tasks does not meaningfully discriminate between trained and randomized transformers in many settings.
Randomly initialized neural networks can preserve or amplify superposition present in input data, which may explain the similar SAE performance.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia models and the RedPajama dataset; results may vary with other architectures or data.
future_direction: Develop better metrics to distinguish between artifacts and genuinely learned computations in interpretability methods.
Investigate why randomly initialized transformers produce SAE metrics similar to trained ones, e.g., whether they preserve or amplify superposition.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to extract sparse, interpretable latents from transformer activations. We test whether commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines can distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones (e.g., where parameters are sampled i.i.d. from a Gaussian). Over a wide range of Pythia model sizes and multiple randomization schemes, we find that, in many settings, SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics that are similar to those from trained models. These results show that high aggregate auto-interpretability scores do not, by themselves, guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered. We therefore recommend treating common SAE metrics as useful but insufficient proxies for mechanistic interpretability and argue for routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.

papers.title: AdaptiveK Sparse Autoencoders: Dynamic Sparsity Allocation for Interpretable LLM Representations
papers.research_question: How can we define semantic simplicity or complexity within LLM representation spaces, and how can this be used to dynamically adjust sparsity in sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaptiveK SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on input complexity, improving reconstruction and interpretability without extensive hyperparameter tuning.
papers.conclusion: AdaptiveK SAE provides an efficient and effective method for interpretable feature extraction in LLMs by dynamically allocating sparsity based on input complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Text complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, as demonstrated by linear probes.
Adaptive sparsity allocation based on complexity improves reconstruction quality and interpretability metrics across multiple model scales.
AdaptiveK SAE outperforms fixed-sparsity baselines on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
papers.limitation: Due to cost constraints, the study used a smaller training dataset (250,000 contexts) compared to the 500,000,000 tokens used in SAEBench.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a central challenge for interpretability research. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising solution by decomposing activations into interpretable features, but existing approaches rely on fixed sparsity constraints that fail to account for input complexity. We propose AdaptiveK SAE (Adaptive Top K Sparse Autoencoders), a novel framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on the semantic complexity of each input. Leveraging linear probes, we demonstrate that context complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, and we use this signal to guide feature allocation during training. Experiments across ten language models (from 70M to 14B parameters) demonstrate that this complexity-driven adaptation significantly outperforms fixed-sparsity approaches on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, cosine similarity and interpretability metrics while eliminating the computational burden of extensive hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we align Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features with human-defined concepts to create an interpretable and controllable interface for Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: ALIGNSAE is a method that aligns Sparse Autoencoder features with a predefined ontology through a two-stage training curriculum, enabling precise concept-level inspection and control in frozen LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ALIGNSAE provides a verifiable and controllable interface for concept-level manipulation in LLMs, advancing interpretability and steering capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ALIGNSAE achieves near-perfect concept-slot binding in mid-layers (e.g., layer 6) of GPT-2, with diagonal accuracy up to 1.00.
It significantly reduces concept fragmentation and increases top-1 concentration compared to traditional unsupervised SAEs.
Swap interventions demonstrate reliable controllability with a clear fidelity-strength tradeoff, achieving up to 0.847 swap success at layer 6.
In 2-hop reasoning, ALIGNSAE attains 4× higher swap success than traditional SAE.
The method provides mechanistic insights into grokking-like generalization dynamics via step-wise concept binding.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on a limited ontology (6 relations for 1-hop, 20 for 2-hop) and on GPT-2, a relatively small model, which may not reflect performance on larger models or more complex ontologies.
Swap controllability has a narrow effective amplification range (around α=2), and over-amplification can destabilize interventions.
future_direction: Extending ALIGNSAE to larger ontologies and more complex concept types.
Applying the method to larger language models and more diverse tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

papers.title: Transferring Linear Features Across Language Models With Model Stitching
papers.research_question: Can linear features (e.g., from Sparse Autoencoders, probes, and steering vectors) be transferred between language models of different sizes using affine mappings (model stitching), and what are the implications for efficiency and feature universality?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that affine mappings (stitches) between residual streams can effectively transfer linear features across language models, enabling compute-efficient training of Sparse Autoencoders and transfer of probes and steering vectors, while revealing differences in how semantic and structural features transfer.
papers.conclusion: Linear features can be transferred between language models via affine mappings, supporting weak universality and providing a method to improve the training efficiency of interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Using transferred SAEs as initialization can reduce FLOPs by ~50% when training SAEs on larger models.
Probes and steering vectors can be transferred between models with no additional training in specific cases (e.g., language steering).
Structural features (syntactic) transfer more consistently than semantic features, which are more polarized in transferability.
Specific functional features (e.g., entropy and attention deactivation features) preserve their roles after transfer.
Linear stitches support a weak universality hypothesis, showing that small and large models learn similar representation spaces.
papers.limitation:
Stitches are only trained on general internet text between models in the same family with the same tokenizer.
The scaling law analysis is theoretically incomplete due to lack of high-compute regime data to fit the irreducible loss.
The semantic/structural classification is imperfect and noisy due to reliance on another LLM for augmentations.
Probing and steering experiments are limited to particular tasks and settings.
future_direction: Verify findings in cross-family model settings and finetune stitches on special tokens or chat-templated data.
Explore other applications of stitches, such as transferring linear weight updates like LoRAs.
Expand probing and steering experiments to examine robustness and broader task settings.
papers.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that affine mappings between residual streams of language models is a cheap way to effectively transfer represented features between models. We apply this technique to transfer the weights of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) between models of different sizes to compare their representations. We find that small and large models learn similar representation spaces, which motivates training expensive components like SAEs on a smaller model and transferring to a larger model at a FLOPs savings. In particular, using a small-to-large transferred SAE as initialization can lead to 50% cheaper training runs when training SAEs on larger models. Next, we show that transferred probes and steering vectors can effectively recover ground truth performance. Finally, we dive deeper into feature-level transferability, finding that semantic and structural features transfer noticeably differently while specific classes of functional features have their roles faithfully mapped. Overall, our findings illustrate similarities and differences in the linear representation spaces of small and large models and demonstrate a method for improving the training efficiency of SAEs.

papers.title: Identifiable Steering via Sparse Autoencoding of Multi-Concept Shifts
papers.research_question: How can we provably recover interpretable concepts from LLM activations in an unsupervised manner, ensuring identifiability to avoid entangled representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Shift Autoencoders (SSAEs), a method that learns sparse representations of differences between embeddings, provably recovering steering vectors for individual concepts from paired observations with multiple unknown concept shifts, under identifiability guarantees.
papers.conclusion: SSAEs offer a provably identifiable approach for unsupervised concept recovery and steering in LLMs, advancing interpretability by ensuring learned representations correspond to genuine underlying concepts.
papers.key_findings:
SSAEs achieve identifiability up to permutation and scaling under assumptions of linear representation and sufficient diversity of multi-concept shifts.
Empirically, SSAEs outperform standard sparse autoencoders and other baselines in Mean Correlation Coefficient (MCC) across synthetic and real-world language datasets.
SSAEs provide more accurate steering, as measured by cosine similarity between steered and target embeddings, especially when concepts are correlated.
SSAE steering vectors generalize better out-of-distribution compared to non-identifiable methods.
The method successfully recovers concepts in real-world tasks such as bias mitigation, truthfulness, sycophancy, and refusal.
papers.limitation:
The identifiability guarantees rely on assumptions such as the Linear Representation Hypothesis and sufficient diversity of multi-concept shifts, which may not hold in all practical settings.
The theoretical analysis assumes the encoder dimension is known (equal to the number of varying concepts |V|), but in practice this is often unknown and a larger dimension is used, which can affect identifiability.
future_direction: Extending the method to non-linear representations.
Applying the approach to other modalities beyond text.
Scaling the method to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: Steering methods manipulate the representations of large language models (LLMs) to induce responses that have desired properties, e.g., truthfulness, offering a promising approach for LLM alignment without the need for fine-tuning. Traditionally, steering has relied on supervision, such as from contrastive pairs of prompts that vary in a single target concept, which is costly to obtain and limits the speed of steering research. An appealing alternative is to use unsupervised approaches such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to map LLM embeddings to sparse representations that capture human-interpretable concepts. However, without further assumptions, SAEs may not be identifiable: they could learn latent dimensions that entangle multiple concepts, leading to unintentional steering of unrelated properties. We introduce Sparse Shift Autoencoders (SSAEs) that instead map the differences between embeddings to sparse representations. Crucially, we show that SSAEs are identifiable from paired observations that vary in \textit{multiple unknown concepts}, leading to accurate steering of single concepts without the need for supervision. We empirically demonstrate accurate steering across semi-synthetic and real-world language datasets using Llama-3.1 embeddings.

papers.title: Toward Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoder (SAE) features capture interpretable signals predictive of hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and how can they be used to build an accurate and interpretable detector?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RAGLens, a lightweight hallucination detector for RAG that uses sparse autoencoder (SAE) features from LLM internal activations, achieving superior detection performance and providing interpretable rationales for its decisions.
papers.conclusion: RAGLens demonstrates that SAE features effectively capture hallucination signals in RAG, enabling accurate, interpretable, and lightweight detection that can generalize across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture nuanced signals specifically activated during RAG hallucinations.
RAGLens outperforms existing methods in detection accuracy on multiple benchmarks and models.
The detector provides interpretable rationales via feature attribution and shape functions, enabling post-hoc mitigation.
RAGLens generalizes across different LLMs and RAG task domains.
Mid-layer SAE features with high mutual information about the labels are most informative for detecting RAG hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models (LLMs) by grounding outputs in retrieved evidence, but faithfulness failures, where generations contradict or extend beyond the provided sources, remain a critical challenge. Existing hallucination detection methods for RAG often rely either on large-scale detector training, which requires substantial annotated data, or on querying external LLM judges, which leads to high inference costs. Although some approaches attempt to leverage internal representations of LLMs for hallucination detection, their accuracy remains limited. Motivated by recent advances in mechanistic interpretability, we employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle internal activations, successfully identifying features that are specifically triggered during RAG hallucinations. Building on a systematic pipeline of information-based feature selection and additive feature modeling, we introduce RAGLens, a lightweight hallucination detector that accurately flags unfaithful RAG outputs using LLM internal representations. RAGLens not only achieves superior detection performance compared to existing methods, but also provides interpretable rationales for its decisions, enabling effective post-hoc mitigation of unfaithful RAG. Finally, we justify our design choices and reveal new insights into the distribution of hallucination-related signals within LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/Teddy-XiongGZ/RAGLens.

papers.title: Interpretable Steering of Large Language Models with Feature Guided Activation Additions
papers.research_question: How can we improve the precision and interpretability of activation steering in large language models by leveraging sparse autoencoder features and optimization techniques?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that uses sparse autoencoder features and optimization to construct precise, interpretable steering vectors, improving steering effectiveness and output coherence compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: FGAA represents a significant step forward in controlled text generation, offering both theoretical insights into activation patterns and practical advances in steering methodology, while highlighting the trade-off between steering strength and capability preservation.
papers.key_findings:
FGAA outperforms existing activation steering methods (CAA, SAE, SAE-TS) on most steering tasks, especially for the Gemma-2-2B model.
FGAA provides more interpretable steering by operating in the SAE feature space and allowing explicit control over which features are steered.
There is a trade-off between steering strength and preservation of model capabilities: all steering methods degrade model performance (perplexity and benchmark accuracy) at high steering scales.
Negative features in steering vectors tend to degrade steering performance, so FGAA focuses on positive features.
The effectiveness of FGAA varies with model size, showing different performance patterns between Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on the quality of feature extraction by the underlying Sparse Autoencoder (SAE).
Optimal selection of n1 and n2 parameters is task-dependent, making universal guidelines challenging.
Developing metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of feature filtering methods is challenging due to the qualitative nature of interpreting features.
future_direction: Investigating how SAE width and quality of SAE features affects steering performance with FGAA.
Exploring techniques to minimize capability degradation at higher steering scales while maintaining steering effectiveness.
Applying FGAA to safety tasks such as controlling sycophancy, hallucination, and refusal in RLHF models and reducing social biases.
papers.abstract: Effective and reliable control over large language model (LLM) behavior is a significant challenge. While activation steering methods, which add steering vectors to a model's hidden states, are a promising approach, existing techniques often lack precision and interpretability in how they influence model outputs. We introduce Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that leverages insights from Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS). By operating in the latent space of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and employing optimization techniques to select desired SAE features, FGAA constructs precise steering vectors that provide better steering effects while maintaining coherence of steered model outputs. In this regard, evaluations on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B models across various steering tasks demonstrate that FGAA outperforms existing steering methods of CAA, SAE decoder steering, and SAE-TS. Our results also highlight important trade-offs between steering scale and general model capabilities that are consistent across all tested steering methods.

papers.title: Group-SAE: Efficient Training of Sparse Autoencoders for Large Language Models via Layer Groups
papers.research_question: How can the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs be reduced while maintaining performance? Specifically, can grouping similar layers and training a single SAE per group achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Group-SAE, a method to reduce the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs by grouping layers with similar residual stream representations and training a single SAE per group, guided by a novel metric called AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance).
papers.conclusion: Group-SAE provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs, achieving significant computational savings without compromising reconstruction quality, downstream task performance, or interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Group-SAE reduces the number of SAEs needed, cutting training costs by up to 50% with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and downstream performance.
The proposed AMAD metric effectively guides the selection of an optimal number of layer groups, balancing efficiency and performance.
Group-SAEs achieve comparable or slightly better interpretability scores (Detection and Fuzzing) than baseline per-layer SAEs.
Features learned by a Group-SAE are most similar to the baseline SAE trained on a layer within its group, and individual features typically peak at a specific layer but spread to adjacent ones.
The method outperforms alternative efficiency baselines like training smaller SAEs on all layers or using evenly spaced groups, especially on downstream performance metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models from the Pythia family trained on the Pile dataset, and the generality to other architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA) or datasets is not evaluated.
The study uses a fixed expansion factor (c=16) and TopK activation function; the impact of these hyperparameter choices is not investigated.
The interpretability evaluation is limited due to the high cost of annotating large numbers of features; a more comprehensive analysis is needed.
future_direction: Further optimizing the number of layer groups and scaling the approach to even larger models.
Evaluating the method on additional datasets and across diverse model architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral).
Conducting a more comprehensive and systematic interpretability analysis.
papers.abstract: Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs) have recently been employed as a promising unsupervised approach for understanding the representations of layers of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, with the growth in model size and complexity, training SAEs is computationally intensive, as typically one SAE is trained for each model layer. To address such limitation, we propose Group-SAE, a novel strategy to train SAEs. Our method considers the similarity of the residual stream representations between contiguous layers to group similar layers and train a single SAE per group. To balance the trade-off between efficiency and performance, we further introduce AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance), an empirical metric that guides the selection of an optimal number of groups based on representational similarity across layers. Experiments on models from the Pythia family show that our approach significantly accelerates training with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and comparable downstream task performance and interpretability over baseline SAEs trained layer by layer. This method provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs.

papers.title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the computational circuits in protein language models that underlie their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoMech, a framework using cross-layer transcoders to discover computational circuits in protein language models, achieving high performance recovery and enabling protein design.
papers.conclusion: ProtoMech establishes a principled framework for protein circuit tracing, revealing interpretable computational pathways and enabling effective protein design.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original ESM2 performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks.
ProtoMech identifies compact circuits using <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.
Steering along the discovered circuits enables high-fitness protein design, outperforming baseline methods in more than 70% of cases.
The circuits correspond to known structural and functional motifs, such as binding sites and catalytic loops.
ProtoMech provides a more accurate approximation of ESM2's computation than per-layer transcoder baselines.
papers.limitation: Full replacement models, where both attention and MLP computations are replaced, lead to substantial performance degradation due to compounding reconstruction errors.
future_direction: Developing robust full replacement models remains an active area of research.
Using a tanh loss for constraining sparsity is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model's full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: The Knowledge Microscope: Features as Better Analytical Lenses than Neurons
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether features (obtained via Sparse Autoencoders) are better analytical units than neurons for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in language models, addressing challenges of limited knowledge expression, poor interpretability, polysemanticity, and performance in downstream tasks like privacy erasure.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that features extracted via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are superior analytical units to neurons for studying factual knowledge in language models, exhibiting stronger impact on knowledge expression, better interpretability, stronger monosemanticity, and enabling more effective privacy erasure through the proposed FeatureEdit method.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that features are better analytical units than neurons for understanding factual knowledge in language models, and the proposed FeatureEdit method effectively leverages features for privacy erasure.
papers.key_findings:
SAE is effective in decomposing neurons into features for studying factual knowledge mechanisms.
Features, especially post-MLP features, have a stronger impact on knowledge expression than neurons.
Features demonstrate superior interpretability compared to neurons.
Features exhibit stronger monosemanticity, with clear activation patterns for related facts and inactivity for unrelated ones.
The proposed feature-based editing method, FeatureEdit, outperforms neuron-based methods in erasing privacy-sensitive knowledge while maintaining better generalization and causing less damage to general model capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mapping from features back to weights is indirect and sub-optimal, requiring reconstruction.
The clustering phenomenon of SAE features and their stability across different numbers of features require further investigation.
future_direction: Investigate the inherent stable structure of SAE feature space and whether it is truly insensitive to the number of features.
Improve the mapping from features back to weights for more direct model editing.
papers.abstract: Previous studies primarily utilize MLP neurons as units of analysis for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in Language Models (LMs); however, neurons suffer from polysemanticity, leading to limited knowledge expression and poor interpretability. In this paper, we first conduct preliminary experiments to validate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) can effectively decompose neurons into features, which serve as alternative analytical units. With this established, our core findings reveal three key advantages of features over neurons: (1) Features exhibit stronger influence on knowledge expression and superior interpretability. (2) Features demonstrate enhanced monosemanticity, showing distinct activation patterns between related and unrelated facts. (3) Features achieve better privacy protection than neurons, demonstrated through our proposed FeatureEdit method, which significantly outperforms existing neuron-based approaches in erasing privacy-sensitive information from LMs.Code and dataset will be available.

papers.title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
papers.research_question: Is the use of nonnegative activations truly essential for the success of SAEs, or does it constrain their ability to capture richer representations? Can SAEs be improved by allowing negative activations, enabling the discovery of bidirectional concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AbsTopK SAE, a sparse autoencoder variant that removes the non-negativity constraint, enabling single latent features to encode bidirectional semantic concepts and improving reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Removing the non-negativity constraint in SAEs via the AbsTopK operator allows single features to capture bipolar semantics and yields reconstructions of superior compactness and fidelity, pioneering a shift towards bipolar sparse representations.
papers.key_findings:
AbsTopK SAE enables single latent features to encode opposing concepts by leveraging both positive and negative activations.
AbsTopK outperforms TopK and JumpReLU SAEs in reconstruction fidelity and interpretability across multiple models and tasks.
AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the supervised Difference-in-Mean method on some steering tasks.
The non-negativity constraint in existing SAEs fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness.
AbsTopK achieves a better balance between safety alignment (HarmBench) and general capability preservation (MMLU) compared to conventional SAE steering.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-step variants, yielding multi-layer encoders that produce more accurate sparse codes.
Investigating JumpReLU variants that apply a threshold on both positive and negative activations.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as powerful techniques for interpretability of large language models (LLMs), aiming to decompose hidden states into meaningful semantic features. While several SAE variants have been proposed, there remains no principled framework to derive SAEs from the original dictionary learning formulation. In this work, we introduce such a framework by unrolling the proximal gradient method for sparse coding. We show that a single-step update naturally recovers common SAE variants, including ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. Through this lens, we reveal a fundamental limitation of existing SAEs: their sparsity-inducing regularizers enforce non-negativity, preventing a single feature from representing bidirectional concepts (e.g., male vs. female). This structural constraint fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness. To address this issue, we propose AbsTopK SAE, a new variant derived from the $\ell_0$ sparsity constraint that applies hard thresholding over the largest-magnitude activations. By preserving both positive and negative activations, AbsTopK uncovers richer, bidirectional conceptual representations. Comprehensive experiments across four LLMs and seven probing and steering tasks show that AbsTopK improves reconstruction fidelity, enhances interpretability, and enables single features to encode contrasting concepts. Remarkably, AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the Difference-in-Mean method, a supervised approach that requires labeled data for each concept and has been shown in prior work to outperform SAEs.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
DSG is highly data-efficient and can perform zero-shot unlearning by leveraging semantically relevant SAE features identified without task-specific data.
DSG provides interpretable unlearning by targeting specific, semantically coherent SAE features associated with the knowledge to be removed.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is a promising approach to improve LLM safety by removing unwanted knowledge from the model. However, prevailing gradient-based unlearning methods suffer from issues such as high computational costs, hyperparameter instability, poor sequential unlearning capability, vulnerability to relearning attacks, low data efficiency, and lack of interpretability. While Sparse Autoencoders are well-suited to improve these aspects by enabling targeted activation-based unlearning, prior approaches underperform gradient-based methods. This work demonstrates that, contrary to these earlier findings, SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when employed dynamically. We introduce $\textbf{Dynamic DAE Guardrails}$ (DSG), a novel method for precision unlearning that leverages principled feature selection and a dynamic classifier. Our experiments show DSG substantially outperforms leading unlearning methods, achieving superior forget-utility trade-offs. DSG addresses key drawbacks of gradient-based approaches for unlearning -- offering enhanced computational efficiency and stability, robust performance in sequential unlearning, stronger resistance to relearning attacks, better data efficiency including zero-shot settings, and more interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
papers.research_question: Does incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improve the reconstruction-interpretability frontier? Specifically, does it improve reconstruction, maintain or improve interpretability, and learn hierarchical semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (H-SAE) architecture that explicitly models semantic hierarchy, improving reconstruction performance and interpretability while being computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improves the reconstruction-interpretability frontier, leading to better reconstruction, maintained or improved interpretability, and learned hierarchical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
H-SAEs have better reconstruction performance than standard SAEs as measured by explained variance and downstream CE loss.
H-SAEs maintain or improve interpretability, showing less feature absorption and fewer redundant features across languages.
The H-SAE architecture learns hierarchical semantics, with high-level features capturing general concepts and low-level features capturing specific instances.
The hierarchical structure provides significant computational efficiency gains, allowing scaling to larger effective dictionary sizes with minimal overhead.
The architecture successfully translates theoretical insights about hierarchical concept geometry into a practical mixture-of-experts type model.
papers.limitation: Results are still imperfect, with some hard-to-interpret features and far from perfect reconstruction.
future_direction: Explore other reconstruction objectives beyond Euclidean distance.
Incorporate insights from causal representation learning into LLM interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.

papers.title: Measuring Progress in Dictionary Learning for Language Model Interpretability with Board Game Models
papers.research_question: How can we measure progress in interpretable dictionary learning for language models? The paper proposes using board game models with known interpretable features as a testbed to evaluate sparse autoencoder quality.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces board game models as a testbed for evaluating sparse autoencoders, proposes two new metrics (coverage and board reconstruction) for SAE quality, and introduces p-annealing, a training technique that improves SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a more objective paradigm for evaluating SAE quality with coverage and board reconstruction metrics, and shows that p-annealing improves SAE training.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can accurately reconstruct game boards, though they do not match linear probe performance.
Standard SAEs trained with p-annealing perform on par with Gated SAEs on existing metrics and show improvement on the new metrics.
Coverage and board reconstruction metrics reveal differences in SAE quality not captured by unsupervised metrics like L0 and loss recovered.
The metrics are optimal in the elbow region of the Pareto frontier, validating common wisdom about SAE quality.
papers.limitation:
The metrics are confined to chess and Othello domains, raising concerns about generalizability.
The set of board state properties is determined by researchers based on domain knowledge, potentially overlooking essential features.
The evaluation does not directly address how learned features could be used for downstream interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: What latent features are encoded in language model (LM) representations? Recent work on training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle interpretable features in LM representations has shown significant promise. However, evaluating the quality of these SAEs is difficult because we lack a ground-truth collection of interpretable features that we expect good SAEs to recover. We thus propose to measure progress in interpretable dictionary learning by working in the setting of LMs trained on chess and Othello transcripts. These settings carry natural collections of interpretable features -- for example, "there is a knight on F3" -- which we leverage into $\textit{supervised}$ metrics for SAE quality. To guide progress in interpretable dictionary learning, we introduce a new SAE training technique, $\textit{p-annealing}$, which improves performance on prior unsupervised metrics as well as our new metrics.

papers.title: AudioSAE: Towards Understanding of Audio-Processing Models with Sparse AutoEncoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be effectively applied to audio-processing models to obtain stable, interpretable features, and do these features have practical utility?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces AudioSAE, applying sparse autoencoders to audio models (Whisper and HuBERT), demonstrating that they yield stable, interpretable features capturing acoustic and semantic information, and shows practical utility in hallucination reduction and correlation with human EEG.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are effective tools for interpreting audio-processing models, providing stable and interpretable features that have practical applications such as hallucination reduction and show alignment with human neural processing.
papers.key_findings:
Over 50% of SAE features remain consistent across random seeds.
SAE features capture general acoustic and semantic information as well as specific events like environmental noises and paralinguistic sounds.
Features disentangle concepts effectively, requiring removal of only 19–27% of features to erase a concept.
Feature steering reduces Whisper’s false speech detections by 70% with negligible WER increase.
SAE features are correlated with human EEG activity during speech perception, indicating alignment with human neural processing.
papers.limitation: The auto-interpretation method depends on empirically selected thresholds and is biased by the predominance of speech data in the test set, potentially obscuring rarer music or sound events, and is limited by the capabilities of the underlying audio captioning model.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are powerful tools for interpreting neural representations, yet their use in audio remains underexplored. We train SAEs across all encoder layers of Whisper and HuBERT, provide an extensive evaluation of their stability, interpretability, and show their practical utility. Over 50% of the features remain consistent across random seeds, and reconstruction quality is preserved. SAE features capture general acoustic and semantic information as well as specific events, including environmental noises and paralinguistic sounds (e.g. laughter, whispering) and disentangle them effectively, requiring removal of only 19-27% of features to erase a concept. Feature steering reduces Whisper's false speech detections by 70% with negligible WER increase, demonstrating real-world applicability. Finally, we find SAE features correlated with human EEG activity during speech perception, indicating alignment with human neural processing. The code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/audiosae/audiosae_demo.

papers.title: TopK Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we build a language model architecture that enjoys the interpretability of sparse autoencoders without suffering the drawbacks of post-hoc training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TopK LMs, a transformer-based language model architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function to achieve inherent, SAE-like interpretability without requiring post-hoc training, while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: TopK LMs represent a significant advance toward trustworthy AI systems by making interpretability a built-in feature, demonstrating that performance and interpretability need not be competing objectives.
papers.key_findings:
TopK LMs achieve competitive language modeling and downstream task performance compared to dense baselines, with only a moderate increase in model size.
Neurons in TopK LMs exhibit higher concept specialization, as measured by lower token and semantic entropy, making them more interpretable.
Single-neuron interventions (activation patching) can causally steer the model's text generation towards specific concepts.
The formation and specialization of individual neurons can be traced continuously across training checkpoints and model layers.
Sparsity annealing during training improves convergence and model performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models up to ~1B parameters; effectiveness on significantly larger models remains an open question.
Evaluation focused on language modeling and standard reasoning benchmarks, leaving performance on specialized downstream tasks unclear.
Long-context modeling capabilities and the interaction between TopK sparsity and attention over long sequences were not examined.
The approach is currently limited to text-only models; extending to multimodal architectures requires future research.
Specific societal applications that could benefit from the model's interpretability were not explored.
future_direction: Scaling the TopK LM approach to significantly larger models (tens or hundreds of billions of parameters).
Extending TopK activation to multimodal architectures combining text with images, audio, or other modalities.
Investigating how TopK LMs can address concrete challenges in model alignment, fairness assessment, safety evaluation, and trustworthy AI deployment.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for analyzing and interpreting the activation space of transformer-based language models (LMs). However, SAEs suffer several shortcomings that diminish their utility and internal validity. Since SAEs are trained post-hoc, it is unclear if the failure to discover a particular concept is a failure on the SAE's side or due to the underlying LM not representing this concept. This problem is exacerbated by training conditions and architecture choices affecting which features an SAE learns. When tracing how LMs learn concepts during training, the lack of feature stability also makes it difficult to compare SAEs features across different checkpoints. To address these limitations, we introduce a modification to the transformer architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function at chosen layers, making the model's hidden states equivalent to the latent features of a TopK SAE. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc training while providing interpretability comparable to SAEs. The resulting TopK LMs offer a favorable trade-off between model size, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Despite this simple architectural change, TopK LMs maintain their original capabilities while providing robust interpretability benefits. Our experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations learned by TopK LMs enable successful steering through targeted neuron interventions and facilitate detailed analysis of neuron formation processes across checkpoints and layers. These features make TopK LMs stable and reliable tools for understanding how language models learn and represent concepts, which we believe will significantly advance future research on model interpretability and controllability.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
