Multi-attribute control with PCA composition strategy yields the best trade-off between control effectiveness and content quality.
Sparse features enable interpretable identification of attribute-relevant dimensions through KL divergence analysis.
papers.limitation: Multi-attribute steering strategies such as PCA may not fully capture complex relationships and conflicts between attributes.
future_direction: Layer-wise or component-wise multi-attribute steering to align interventions with semantic levels.
Context-aware and personalized steering based on semantic subdomains of prompts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities in generation tasks but are prone to producing harmful, misleading, or biased content, posing significant ethical and safety concerns. To mitigate such risks, representation engineering, which steer model behavior toward desired attributes by injecting carefully designed steering vectors into LLM's representations at inference time, has emerged as a promising alternative to fine-tuning approaches. However, due to the semantically entangled nature of LLM's representation, existing representation engineering methods still suffer from several limitations: limited fine-grained controllability, content quality degradation, and conflict in multi-attribute control. To overcome these challenges, we propose Sparse Representation Steering (SRS), a novel framework that achieves fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior by first disentangling internal activations into a sparse, semantically meaningful representation space, and then selectively steering relevant dimensions. Specifically, SRS leverages a pretrained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to transform dense, entangled activation patterns into a sparse monosemantic feature space. To identify relevant features, SRS contrasts sparse activations from positive and negative prompt pairs and measures their bidirectional KL divergence to locate dimensions most associated with the target attribute. We conduct comprehensive experiments on Gemma-2 series model across three alignment dimensions, i.e., safety, fairness, and truthfulness, to evaluate the effectiveness of SRS. Results show that SRS consistently outperforms existing steering methods, which achieves significantly improved controllability across both single and multiple attribute settings, while preserving high linguistic quality and general ability.

papers.title: Low-Rank Adapting Models for Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can language models be optimized after sparse autoencoder (SAE) training to improve the interpretability vs. performance trade-off, specifically by using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to reduce the cross-entropy loss gap when SAE reconstructions are inserted?
papers.core_contribution: Using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to finetune a language model around a pre-trained sparse autoencoder (SAE) significantly reduces the cross-entropy loss gap when the SAE is inserted, improving the interpretability-performance trade-off efficiently.
papers.conclusion: Low-rank adapting models for SAEs provides a fast, cheap, and effective path to producing interpretable combined model and SAE systems, challenging the assumption that interpretability improvements must rely solely on post-hoc model decomposition.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA adaptation reduces the cross entropy loss gap (L_SAE - L_BASE) by 30% to 55% across various SAE sparsities, widths, model sizes, and layers.
The method achieves the same downstream cross entropy loss as end-to-end (e2e) SAEs 2× to 20× faster on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B.
Adapting multiple SAEs at once significantly reduces the compound cross entropy loss, making the technique promising for circuit analysis.
The method improves downstream SAE metrics on SAEBench and a novel feature steering evaluation without harming general language model capabilities on benchmarks like MMLU and HellaSwag.
Much of the loss reduction can be achieved by training adapters only on the layer immediately after the SAE, suggesting a relatively simple improvement mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability work usually interprets a frozen model, while this work changes it; for some applications, this might not be acceptable.
The work does not yet show that the technique helps discover more faithful circuits for model behaviors.
The end-to-end (e2e) SAE baselines may not have fully converged in the experiments, limiting the comparison of converged accuracy.
Fixed learning rates were used for e2e SAE training; further tuning could potentially improve their training speed.
future_direction: Showing that the technique helps discover more faithful circuits for model behaviors.
Further exploration of language model modifications to improve interpretability, building on the degrees of freedom provided by modifying the entire model.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model representations into a sparse set of linear latent vectors. Recent works have improved SAEs using language model gradients, but these techniques require many expensive backward passes during training and still cause a significant increase in cross entropy loss when SAE reconstructions are inserted into the model. In this work, we improve on these limitations by taking a fundamentally different approach: we use low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to finetune the \textit{language model itself} around a previously trained SAE. We analyze our method across SAE sparsity, SAE width, language model size, LoRA rank, and model layer on the Gemma Scope family of SAEs. In these settings, our method reduces the cross entropy loss gap by 30\% to 55\% when SAEs are inserted during the forward pass. We also find that compared to end-to-end (e2e) SAEs, our approach achieves the same downstream cross entropy loss 3$\times$ to 20$\times$ faster on \gemma and 2$\times$ to 10$\times$ faster on \llama. We further show that our technique improves downstream metrics and can adapt multiple SAEs at once without harming general language model capabilities. Our results demonstrate that improving model interpretability is not limited to post-hoc SAE training; Pareto improvements can also be achieved by directly optimizing the model itself.

papers.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
papers.research_question: How to effectively steer LLMs for safety by capturing distributed safety representations using graph-regularized sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAE) to capture distributed safety representations in LLMs, enabling effective runtime safety steering with high refusal rates and preserved utility.
papers.conclusion: GSAE provides a robust method for safety steering by learning distributed safety representations, achieving high safety discrimination and utility preservation across diverse models and attacks.
papers.key_findings:
GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%).
It maintains strong task accuracy on QA benchmarks (e.g., 70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K).
GSAE generalizes across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and scales.
It is robust against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining ≥90% refusal of harmful content.
Ablation studies show that graph regularization is essential for performance, and the dual-gating mechanism enables adaptive steering.
papers.limitation: The runtime steering mechanism incurs inference latency overhead, which can interfere with optimized serving engines.
future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: Finding the Translation Switch: Discovering and Exploiting the Task-Initiation Features in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanism within instruction-tuned models is responsible for the innate translation ability of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to identify 'translation initiation' features in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders and demonstrates their causal role; proposes a mechanistic data selection strategy for efficient fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The paper decodes the translation initiation features in LLMs and shows how mechanistic insights can be used for efficient fine-tuning and specialization.
papers.key_findings:
A small set of 'translation initiation' features are causally responsible for the model's translation ability.
Amplifying these features improves translation quality and reduces hallucinations across diverse language pairs.
These features are language-agnostic and generalize across different translation directions.
A data selection strategy that prioritizes 'mechanistically hard' samples (low activation of initiation features) improves fine-tuning efficiency and reduces hallucinations.
The identified mechanisms are transferable across scales within the same model family but not across different architectures.
papers.limitation: The translation initiation features are not transferable across different model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit strong translation abilities, even without task-specific fine-tuning. However, the internal mechanisms governing this innate capability remain largely opaque. To demystify this process, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and introduce a novel framework for identifying task-specific features. Our method first recalls features that are frequently co-activated on translation inputs and then filters them for functional coherence using a PCA-based consistency metric. This framework successfully isolates a small set of **translation initiation** features. Causal interventions demonstrate that amplifying these features steers the model towards correct translation, while ablating them induces hallucinations and off-task outputs, confirming they represent a core component of the model's innate translation competency. Moving from analysis to application, we leverage this mechanistic insight to propose a new data selection strategy for efficient fine-tuning. Specifically, we prioritize training on **mechanistically hard** samples-those that fail to naturally activate the translation initiation features. Experiments show this approach significantly improves data efficiency and suppresses hallucinations. Furthermore, we find these mechanisms are transferable to larger models of the same family. Our work not only decodes a core component of the translation mechanism in LLMs but also provides a blueprint for using internal model mechanism to create more robust and efficient models. The codes are available at https://github.com/flamewei123/AAAI26-translation-Initiation-Features.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Targeted Concept Erasure Tasks
papers.research_question: How can we develop effective evaluation metrics for Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) that measure their ability to disentangle concepts and remove spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces two evaluation metrics for Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs): an automated version of SHIFT and the novel Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) metric, which measure SAEs' ability to disentangle and causally isolate concepts.
papers.conclusion: SHIFT and TPP are effective, computationally efficient metrics for evaluating SAEs that can be applied to a wide range of datasets and show improvement during training, but they should be used as part of a broader evaluation suite due to their limitations.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT and TPP effectively differentiate between SAE architectures, with TopK and JumpReLU outperforming Standard SAEs.
Both metrics show improvement throughout SAE training, with most gains in the first 10% of training.
The metrics can be computed efficiently without an LLM judge, but using an LLM judge increases confidence and correlates well with the unfiltered versions.
The optimal sparsity for each metric differs, indicating a trade-off between sparsity and performance.
A single TopK SAE can achieve better performance on SHIFT than multiple Standard SAEs, as shown in the Pythia-70M experiments.
papers.limitation:
The LLM judge has a lower bar for interpretability than standard automated interpretability methods, potentially leading to false negatives.
The evaluation metrics rely on subjective hypotheses about human-understandable concepts, which may not reflect the model's true internal representations.
Hyperparameter selection and SAE latent selection are challenging due to lack of ground truth and variability across model sizes.
The metrics focus on causal isolation of concepts, but high-quality SAEs should also exhibit other characteristics like sparsity and disentanglement.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are an interpretability technique aimed at decomposing neural network activations into interpretable units. However, a major bottleneck for SAE development has been the lack of high-quality performance metrics, with prior work largely relying on unsupervised proxies. In this work, we introduce a family of evaluations based on SHIFT, a downstream task from Marks et al. (Sparse Feature Circuits, 2024) in which spurious cues are removed from a classifier by ablating SAE features judged to be task-irrelevant by a human annotator. We adapt SHIFT into an automated metric of SAE quality; this involves replacing the human annotator with an LLM. Additionally, we introduce the Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) metric that quantifies an SAE's ability to disentangle similar concepts, effectively scaling SHIFT to a wider range of datasets. We apply both SHIFT and TPP to multiple open-source models, demonstrating that these metrics effectively differentiate between various SAE training hyperparameters and architectures.

papers.title: The Geometry of Concepts: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Structure
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of sparse autoencoder features at atomic, intermediate, and large scales?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features exhibit geometric structure at three scales: atomic crystal structures (parallelograms/trapezoids), intermediate functional lobes (e.g., for math and code), and large-scale anisotropic point clouds with power-law eigenvalue spectra.
papers.conclusion: SAE features have geometric structure at multiple scales, which may help understand how networks represent features and improve AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Atomic-scale crystal structures (parallelograms/trapezoids) are revealed after projecting out distractor features using linear discriminant analysis (LDA).
Intermediate-scale functional lobes exist where co-occurring features (e.g., math and code features) cluster together spatially, quantified by mutual information and classification accuracy.
Large-scale point cloud structure is anisotropic with a power-law eigenvalue spectrum, steepest in middle layers.
Clustering entropy (negentropy) is lower in middle layers, indicating more structured representations.
The eigenvalue spectrum of SAE features decays as a power law, more steeply than for raw activations.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain why the observed geometric structure forms.
future_direction: Further work to explain the origin of the geometric structure in SAE features.
Investigate whether variations in structure across layers depend on the prominence of crystals or lobes or have a different origin.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders have recently produced dictionaries of high-dimensional vectors corresponding to the universe of concepts represented by large language models. We find that this concept universe has interesting structure at three levels: 1) The "atomic" small-scale structure contains "crystals" whose faces are parallelograms or trapezoids, generalizing well-known examples such as (man-woman-king-queen). We find that the quality of such parallelograms and associated function vectors improves greatly when projecting out global distractor directions such as word length, which is efficiently done with linear discriminant analysis. 2) The "brain" intermediate-scale structure has significant spatial modularity; for example, math and code features form a "lobe" akin to functional lobes seen in neural fMRI images. We quantify the spatial locality of these lobes with multiple metrics and find that clusters of co-occurring features, at coarse enough scale, also cluster together spatially far more than one would expect if feature geometry were random. 3) The "galaxy" scale large-scale structure of the feature point cloud is not isotropic, but instead has a power law of eigenvalues with steepest slope in middle layers. We also quantify how the clustering entropy depends on the layer.

papers.title: What can attribution methods show us about chemical language models?
papers.research_question: How can attribution methods be used to explain the predictions of a chemical language model for aqueous solubility?
papers.core_contribution: The adapted transformer-specific attribution method produces sparse attributions that reflect how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, while SHAP provides sensible atom-level attributions but fails to explain functional groups relevant to solubility.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods provide insight into how chemical language models represent molecules, but current techniques have limitations in explaining solubility predictions in terms of functional groups, instead revealing how the model organizes its latent space.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning the MegaMolBART encoder significantly improves aqueous solubility prediction accuracy.
The transformer-specific attribution method (using the hRi token) yields sparse attributions that are characteristic of how the model represents molecular similarity in its latent space.
SHAP provides chemically sensible attributions (e.g., highlighting electronegative atoms) but does not explain predictions at the level of functional groups.
The fine-tuned model's latent space becomes linearly separable with respect to solubility along the first principal component.
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, limiting its ability to attribute negative contributions to solubility.
papers.limitation:
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, preventing attribution of features that negatively contribute to solubility.
SHAP does not capture functional group-level explanations for solubility predictions.
ECFP-based models are less predictive and their explanations are coarse-grained.
future_direction: Using the attributions to design focused, informative chemical datasets by creating training examples that contravene the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Language models trained on molecular string representations have shown strong performance in predictive and generative tasks. However, practical applications require not only making accurate predictions, but also explainability - the ability to explain the reasons and rationale behind the predictions. In this work, we explore explainability for a chemical language model by adapting a transformer-specific and a model-agnostic input attribution technique. We fine-tune a pretrained model to predict aqueous solubility, compare training and architecture variants, and evaluate visualizations of attributed relevance. The model-agnostic SHAP technique provides sensible attributions, highlighting the positive influence of individual electronegative atoms, but does not explain the model in terms of functional groups or explain how the model represents molecular strings internally to make predictions. In contrast, the adapted transformer-specific explainability technique produces sparse attributions, which cannot be directly attributed to functional groups relevant to solubility. Instead, the attributions are more characteristic of how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, which seems to represent features relevant to molecular similarity rather than functional groups. These findings provide insight into the representations underpinning chemical language models, which we propose may be leveraged for the design of informative chemical spaces for training more accurate, advanced and explainable models.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Adaptive Sparse Allocation with Mutual Choice & Feature Choice Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to allow adaptive computation and reduce dead features by variable allocation of sparsity budget per token and per feature?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs, which allow adaptive computation by variable allocation of sparsity budget, and aux_zipf_loss, reducing dead features and improving reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs are simple drop-in improvements that enable adaptive computation and reduce dead features, advancing sparse autoencoder training for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs achieve better reconstruction loss at equivalent sparsity levels compared to TopK SAEs.
Feature Choice SAEs result in zero dead features even at large scale, without complex resampling.
The aux_zipf_loss mitigates underutilized features and helps utilize SAE capacity more fully.
Feature densities in SAEs tend to follow a Zipf distribution, and constraining with Zipf distribution outperforms uniform distribution.
Adaptive computation allows difficult tokens to use more features and easy tokens to use fewer.
papers.limitation:
Appeals to the Monotonic Importance Heuristic may miss important low-magnitude activations.
Generalisation across modalities (e.g., audio, images) is untested.
Lack of widely agreed upon metrics for evaluating sparse autoencoders.
future_direction: Scaling laws for Feature Choice SAE performance on larger models.
Dissecting phenomenology of features conditioning on prevalence and activation magnitude.
Applying similar techniques to interpretability problems in other modalities.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach to extracting features from neural networks, enabling model interpretability as well as causal interventions on model internals. SAEs generate sparse feature representations using a sparsifying activation function that implicitly defines a set of token-feature matches. We frame the token-feature matching as a resource allocation problem constrained by a total sparsity upper bound. For example, TopK SAEs solve this allocation problem with the additional constraint that each token matches with at most $k$ features. In TopK SAEs, the $k$ active features per token constraint is the same across tokens, despite some tokens being more difficult to reconstruct than others. To address this limitation, we propose two novel SAE variants, Feature Choice SAEs and Mutual Choice SAEs, which each allow for a variable number of active features per token. Feature Choice SAEs solve the sparsity allocation problem under the additional constraint that each feature matches with at most $m$ tokens. Mutual Choice SAEs solve the unrestricted allocation problem where the total sparsity budget can be allocated freely between tokens and features. Additionally, we introduce a new auxiliary loss function, $\mathtt{aux\_zipf\_loss}$, which generalises the $\mathtt{aux\_k\_loss}$ to mitigate dead and underutilised features. Our methods result in SAEs with fewer dead features and improved reconstruction loss at equivalent sparsity levels as a result of the inherent adaptive computation. More accurate and scalable feature extraction methods provide a path towards better understanding and more precise control of foundation models.

papers.title: Uncovering Cross-Linguistic Disparities in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What are the systematic activation disparities between high-resource and medium-to-low resource languages in multilingual LLMs, and can activation-aware fine-tuning reduce these disparities and improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals systematic activation disparities in multilingual LLMs, where medium-to-low resource languages receive significantly lower activations, and demonstrates that activation-aware fine-tuning can reduce these disparities and lead to modest improvements in benchmark performance.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic activation disparities across languages despite embedding similarity, and while fine-tuning reduces activation gaps, its effect on task performance remains limited, highlighting the need for more effective adaptation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Medium-to-low resource languages exhibit up to 26.27% lower activations in early layers compared to high-resource languages, with a persistent gap of 19.89% in deeper layers.
Activation disparities are correlated with performance gaps on multilingual benchmarks (ARC-C, MMLU, HellaSwag).
Activation-aware fine-tuning via LoRA substantially increases activations for medium-to-low resource languages (e.g., 87.69% for Malayalam) while retaining English activations at ~91%.
Fine-tuning leads to modest but consistent improvements in benchmark performance, such as a 1.44-point increase in ARC-C accuracy for Malayalam.
Embedding similarity does not guarantee equitable activation dynamics or performance, challenging the assumption that it indicates equal linguistic understanding.
papers.limitation:
Translation errors from Helsinki-NLP models may introduce bias and misalign activation patterns, particularly for medium-to-low resource languages.
Benchmark performance improvements from fine-tuning are modest, suggesting activation alignment alone is insufficient for full convergence to shared representations.
Findings are based on Gemma-2-2B, and it remains unclear whether similar activation disparities exist across other model architectures.
future_direction: Refining fine-tuning techniques to better translate activation alignment into performance gains.
Extending the analysis to other LLMs and multilingual datasets to further improve language equity in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong cross-linguistic generalization, yet medium to low resource languages underperform on common benchmarks such as ARC-Challenge, MMLU, and HellaSwag. We analyze activation patterns in Gemma-2-2B across all 26 residual layers and 10 languages: Chinese (zh), Russian (ru), Spanish (es), Italian (it), medium to low resource languages including Indonesian (id), Catalan (ca), Marathi (mr), Malayalam (ml), and Hindi (hi), with English (en) as the reference. Using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), we reveal systematic disparities in activation patterns. Medium to low resource languages receive up to 26.27 percent lower activations in early layers, with a persistent gap of 19.89 percent in deeper layers. To address this, we apply activation-aware fine-tuning via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), leading to substantial activation gains, such as 87.69 percent for Malayalam and 86.32 percent for Hindi, while maintaining English retention at approximately 91 percent. After fine-tuning, benchmark results show modest but consistent improvements, highlighting activation alignment as a key factor in enhancing multilingual LLM performance.

papers.title: LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we precisely identify and modify latent feature representations to improve the semantic consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) when responding to semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LF-Steering, a novel activation steering method that uses a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to decompose transformer layer hidden states into a sparsely activated, higher-dimensional feature space, enabling precise identification and adjustment of features responsible for semantic inconsistency to improve LLM performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LF-Steering method effectively enhances the semantic consistency of LLMs by enabling precise, feature-level activation steering, leading to significant task performance gains across a range of NLU and NLG datasets.
papers.key_findings:
LF-Steering achieves state-of-the-art performance in enhancing semantic consistency, outperforming baseline activation steering methods on NLU and NLG tasks.
Feature-level steering using SAE features significantly outperforms neuron-level (hidden state) steering, demonstrating the advantage of operating on decoupled feature representations.
The method shows good locality, not negatively impacting performance on out-of-domain datasets and sometimes improving it.
Middle to final transformer layers (layers 17-32 in LLama2-7B-Chat) are most significantly associated with semantic inconsistency.
The effectiveness of the method depends on selecting appropriate hyperparameters, such as the feature difference threshold and steering strength.
papers.limitation: Addressing semantic inconsistency at a single transformer layer may offer only a partial solution, as relevant latent representations may span multiple layers.
future_direction: Focus on identifying and steering circuits across multiple transformer layers to enhance the LLM's semantic consistency.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate inconsistent responses when prompted with semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs. Recently, activation steering, a technique that modulates LLMs' behaviours by adjusting their latent representations during inference time, has been explored to improve the semantic consistency of LLMs. However, these methods typically operate at the model component level, such as layer hidden states or attention head outputs. They face a challenge due to the ``polysemanticity issue'', where the model components of LLMs typically encode multiple entangled features, making precise steering difficult. To address this challenge, we drill down to feature-level representations and propose LF-Steering, a novel activation steering approach to precisely identify latent feature representations responsible for semantic inconsistency. More specifically, our method maps the hidden states of the relevant transformer layer into a sparsely activated, high-dimensional feature space based on a sparse autoencoder (SAE), ensuring model steering based on decoupled feature representations with minimal interference. Comprehensive experiments on NLU and NLG datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in enhancing semantic consistency, resulting in significant performance gains for various NLU and NLG tasks.

papers.title: SplInterp: Improving our Understanding and Training of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the theoretical understanding and training of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) using spline theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies spline theory to understand SAEs, showing they are piecewise affine splines that generalize k-means autoencoders, and introduces the PAM-SGD training algorithm which improves sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.conclusion: The spline theory lens provides insight into SAEs, and PAM-SGD is a promising training method with advantages in sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs are piecewise affine splines, and TopK SAEs correspond to Kth-order power diagrams.
SAEs generalize k-means autoencoders but sacrifice accuracy for interpretability compared to the optimal piecewise affine autoencoder (which combines k-means with local PCA).
The proposed PAM-SGD algorithm for training SAEs has solid theoretical foundations and shows promising empirical results, especially in low-data regimes and improved sparsity.
papers.limitation:
The spline geometry characterization is currently limited to TopK SAEs.
The bridge between SAEs and PCA-based autoencoders sets aside the matter of shared decoding vectors.
PAM-SGD makes approximations that break assumptions of the theory and had some empirical limitations (e.g., instability with TopK in LLM experiments).
future_direction: Extending the spline geometry characterization beyond TopK SAEs.
Exploring the incorporation of geometry into SAE training.
Studying the optimal autoencoding with shared decoding vectors and understanding more deeply the pros and cons of PAM-SGD.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have received considerable recent attention as tools for mechanistic interpretability, showing success at extracting interpretable features even from very large LLMs. However, this research has been largely empirical, and there have been recent doubts about the true utility of SAEs. In this work, we seek to enhance the theoretical understanding of SAEs, using the spline theory of deep learning. By situating SAEs in this framework: we discover that SAEs generalise ``$k$-means autoencoders'' to be piecewise affine, but sacrifice accuracy for interpretability vs. the optimal ``$k$-means-esque plus local principal component analysis (PCA)'' piecewise affine autoencoder. We characterise the underlying geometry of (TopK) SAEs using power diagrams. And we develop a novel proximal alternating method SGD (PAM-SGD) algorithm for training SAEs, with both solid theoretical foundations and promising empirical results in MNIST and LLM experiments, particularly in sample efficiency and (in the LLM setting) improved sparsity of codes. All code is available at: https://github.com/splInterp2025/splInterp

papers.title: Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
papers.research_question: How can we control fine-grained reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models using Sparse Autoencoders to overcome concept entanglement and improve reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-Steering, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders to disentangle and identify strategy-specific features for controlling reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models, achieving superior control effectiveness and error correction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can disentangle strategy-specific features for fine-grained control of reasoning strategies, with SAE-Steering providing an efficient feature identification pipeline that is effective and robust.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Steering outperforms existing control methods by over 15% in control effectiveness across various reasoning tasks and models.
The identified SAE features generalize from math to science domains, indicating cross-domain applicability.
Logit-based feature recall is more precise than activation-based methods, improving feature selection accuracy.
Strategy-specific features are prevalent in deeper layers of the model, with optimal control effectiveness in middle-to-late layers.
Controlling reasoning strategies can redirect models from erroneous paths, achieving a 7% absolute accuracy improvement in error correction.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated five representative reasoning strategies
Only demonstrated application in error correction scenarios
Only attempted to correct erroneous paths by enforcing continued reasoning
future_direction: Investigate controlling other reasoning strategies
Explore applying control to a wider range of applications
Explore guiding the LRM at earlier stages or during intermediate steps
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit human-like cognitive reasoning strategies (e.g. backtracking, cross-verification) during reasoning process, which improves their performance on complex tasks. Currently, reasoning strategies are autonomously selected by LRMs themselves. However, such autonomous selection often produces inefficient or even erroneous reasoning paths. To make reasoning more reliable and flexible, it is important to develop methods for controlling reasoning strategies. Existing methods struggle to control fine-grained reasoning strategies due to conceptual entanglement in LRMs' hidden states. To address this, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose strategy-entangled hidden states into a disentangled feature space. To identify the few strategy-specific features from the vast pool of SAE features, we propose SAE-Steering, an efficient two-stage feature identification pipeline. SAE-Steering first recalls features that amplify the logits of strategy-specific keywords, filtering out over 99\% of features, and then ranks the remaining features by their control effectiveness. Using the identified strategy-specific features as control vectors, SAE-Steering outperforms existing methods by over 15\% in control effectiveness. Furthermore, controlling reasoning strategies can redirect LRMs from erroneous paths to correct ones, achieving a 7\% absolute accuracy improvement.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Unveiling Decision-Making in LLMs for Text Classification : Extraction of influential and interpretable concepts with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) based explainability approaches for sentence classification, and can a novel supervised SAE variant (ClassifSAE) improve the causality and interpretability of extracted concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ClassifSAE, a supervised Sparse Autoencoder variant for text classification that extracts more interpretable and causal concepts from LLMs, and proposes two new metrics (ConceptSim and SentenceSim) for evaluating concept precision.
papers.conclusion: ClassifSAE is an effective method for extracting interpretable and causal concepts from LLMs for text classification, offering a good trade-off between interpretability and causality.
papers.key_findings:
ClassifSAE produces concepts with higher interpretability (ConceptSim) and better sparsity than baselines.
ClassifSAE achieves second-best causality scores (after HI-Concept) but with better interpretability.
ClassifSAE is computationally more efficient, requiring up to 83% less training time than HI-Concept.
The joint classifier and activation rate sparsity loss in ClassifSAE improve disentanglement and sparsity of concepts.
ClassifSAE can identify fine-grained concepts beyond coarse label categories.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been successfully used to probe Large Language Models (LLMs) and extract interpretable concepts from their internal representations. These concepts are linear combinations of neuron activations that correspond to human-interpretable features. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of SAE-based explainability approaches for sentence classification, a domain where such methods have not been extensively explored. We present a novel SAE-based model ClassifSAE tailored for text classification, leveraging a specialized classifier head and incorporating an activation rate sparsity loss. We benchmark this architecture against established methods such as ConceptShap, Independent Component Analysis, HI-Concept and a standard TopK-SAE baseline. Our evaluation covers several classification benchmarks and backbone LLMs. We further enrich our analysis with two novel metrics for measuring the precision of concept-based explanations, using an external sentence encoder. Our empirical results show that ClassifSAE improves both the causality and interpretability of the extracted features.

papers.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What causes Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to fail in recovering true underlying features when the features form a hierarchy? The paper identifies and studies the phenomenon of feature absorption.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of feature absorption in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), showing it is caused by hierarchical features and the sparsity penalty, and introduces a metric to detect it.
papers.conclusion: Feature absorption poses an obstacle to the practical application of SAEs for interpretability, and fundamental theoretical issues need to be addressed before SAEs can be used robustly at scale.
papers.key_findings:
Feature absorption occurs in SAEs when features form a hierarchy, causing seemingly monosemantic latents to fail to fire where they should.
The phenomenon is caused by the sparsity penalty in SAEs.
The paper proposes a metric to detect feature absorption and validates it on hundreds of LLM SAEs.
Feature absorption is widespread and occurs in every LLM SAE tested.
Varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve the issue.
papers.limitation:
The absorption metric is limited to early layers (before layer 18 in Gemma 2 2B) because attention moves information to later tokens, making causal interventions ineffective at later layers.
The absorption metric is likely an underestimate of true absorption because it only captures cases where a single latent dominates and the main latents are fully turned off.
future_direction: Develop improved metrics for feature absorption that can be applied at all model layers and capture partial absorption.
Address the fundamental theoretical issues causing feature absorption to enable robust use of SAEs for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) aim to decompose the activation space of large language models (LLMs) into human-interpretable latent directions or features. As we increase the number of features in the SAE, hierarchical features tend to split into finer features ("math" may split into "algebra", "geometry", etc.), a phenomenon referred to as feature splitting. However, we show that sparse decomposition and splitting of hierarchical features is not robust. Specifically, we show that seemingly monosemantic features fail to fire where they should, and instead get "absorbed" into their children features. We coin this phenomenon feature absorption, and show that it is caused by optimizing for sparsity in SAEs whenever the underlying features form a hierarchy. We introduce a metric to detect absorption in SAEs, and validate our findings empirically on hundreds of LLM SAEs. Our investigation suggests that varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve this issue. We discuss the implications of feature absorption in SAEs and some potential approaches to solve the fundamental theoretical issues before SAEs can be used for interpreting LLMs robustly and at scale.

papers.title: CRISP: Persistent Concept Unlearning via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to achieve persistent concept unlearning in large language models using sparse autoencoders to remove harmful knowledge while maintaining model utility.
papers.core_contribution: CRISP is a parameter-efficient method for persistent concept unlearning in LLMs using sparse autoencoders, achieving state-of-the-art performance by selectively suppressing harmful features while preserving benign knowledge and fluency.
papers.conclusion: CRISP is an effective sparse autoencoder-based method for persistent unlearning in LLMs, offering improved performance and interpretability through feature-level suppression.
papers.key_findings:
CRISP outperforms prior methods like ELM and RMU on WMDP benchmarks, with higher overall scores.
It maintains better fluency and concept scores after unlearning, as shown in qualitative and quantitative evaluations.
Feature analysis reveals that CRISP identifies semantically coherent target features for suppression, enabling precise unlearning.
CRISP demonstrates a superior trade-off between unlearning efficacy and retention of benign knowledge.
The method is effective across different models, including Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B.
papers.limitation:
Relies on pretrained SAEs, and effectiveness may diminish if SAEs fail to capture disentangled or interpretable features.
Evaluation is limited to safety-critical domains, and generalization to new tasks and domains is not yet understood.
No formal theoretical guarantees of complete knowledge removal; residual information may persist, and robustness against adversarial extraction is an open direction.
future_direction: Robustness against adversarial extraction
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the need to selectively remove unwanted knowledge while preserving model utility has become paramount. Recent work has explored sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to perform precise interventions on monosemantic features. However, most SAE-based methods operate at inference time, which does not create persistent changes in the model's parameters. Such interventions can be bypassed or reversed by malicious actors with parameter access. We introduce CRISP, a parameter-efficient method for persistent concept unlearning using SAEs. CRISP automatically identifies salient SAE features across multiple layers and suppresses their activations. We experiment with two LLMs and show that our method outperforms prior approaches on safety-critical unlearning tasks from the WMDP benchmark, successfully removing harmful knowledge while preserving general and in-domain capabilities. Feature-level analysis reveals that CRISP achieves semantically coherent separation between target and benign concepts, allowing precise suppression of the target features.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Insights Into the Inner Workings of Transformer Models for Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How can explainable AI methods be extended to inspect latent representations in transformer models for protein function prediction, and do the identified relevant sequence parts reflect biological expectations?
papers.core_contribution: Extends integrated gradients to compute head-specific attributions in transformers for protein function prediction, showing that attribution maps correlate with biological sequence annotations and identifying specialized heads.
papers.conclusion: The extended integrated gradients method provides insights into transformer models for protein function prediction, showing that models focus on biologically relevant sequence parts and that specific heads are specialized for certain annotations.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution maps at the embedding layer correlate significantly with UniProt annotations for EC classes and GO membrane term.
Inside the model, specific transformer heads show significant correlation between attributions and annotations, indicating specialization.
For GO membrane term, heads with positive relevance and correlation with transmembrane regions are identified.
For GO catalytic activity, heads correlate with active sites and PROSITE patterns.
The method is sensitive to model parameters and provides insights beyond anecdotal evidence.
papers.limitation: The method may identify significant heads due to coincidental partial alignment of randomly initialized heads with directions in feature space that happen to correlate with sequence annotations.
papers.abstract: Motivation: We explored how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can help to shed light into the inner workings of neural networks for protein function prediction, by extending the widely used XAI method of integrated gradients such that latent representations inside of transformer models, which were finetuned to Gene Ontology term and Enzyme Commission number prediction, can be inspected too. Results: The approach enabled us to identify amino acids in the sequences that the transformers pay particular attention to, and to show that these relevant sequence parts reflect expectations from biology and chemistry, both in the embedding layer and inside of the model, where we identified transformer heads with a statistically significant correspondence of attribution maps with ground truth sequence annotations (e.g. transmembrane regions, active sites) across many proteins. Availability and Implementation: Source code can be accessed at https://github.com/markuswenzel/xai-proteins .

papers.title: SAFE: A Sparse Autoencoder-Based Framework for Robust Query Enrichment and Hallucination Mitigation in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we harness the creative power of LLMs while mitigating their hallucinations by steering the model to leverage its existing knowledge more effectively using Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAFE, a two-stage framework that first detects hallucinations via entropy-based uncertainty estimation and then mitigates them by enriching the query with SAE-derived features, improving accuracy without additional training.
papers.conclusion: SAFE significantly reduces hallucination rates and improves response accuracy by up to 29.45% in a training-free, plug-and-play manner, offering a practical solution for enhancing LLM reliability.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE improves accuracy on hallucination-prone QA datasets across different models and architectures.
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of entropy-based detection and SAE-driven enrichment in achieving performance gains.
SAFE can make smaller models perform comparably to larger ones in some cases, as shown by the comparison with Gemma2-27b and Llama3-70b.
The framework operates in a training-free manner, offering a lightweight, plug-and-play solution.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on an SAE and the availability of auto-interpretable features constrains its applicability to LLMs that expose such internal representations.
Effectiveness is influenced by the quality of the input queries.
Current implementation is restricted to English-language inputs.
future_direction: Extending the approach to models without SAE characteristics would require modifications or alternative interpretability techniques.
Multilingual and multimodal extensions are promising directions for future research.
papers.abstract: Despite the state-of-the-art performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), these models often suffer from hallucinations, which can undermine their performance in critical applications. In this work, we propose SAFE, a novel method for detecting and mitigating hallucinations by leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). While hallucination detection techniques and SAEs have been explored independently, their synergistic application in a comprehensive system, particularly for hallucination-aware query enrichment, has not been fully investigated. To validate the effectiveness of SAFE, we evaluate it on two models with available SAEs across three diverse cross-domain datasets designed to assess hallucination problems. Empirical results demonstrate that SAFE consistently improves query generation accuracy and mitigates hallucinations across all datasets, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 29.45%.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Kronecker Factorization Improves Efficiency and Interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the computational efficiency and interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for language model interpretation? Specifically, can a Kronecker-factorized encoder with a novel activation function reduce costs while maintaining reconstruction quality and yielding more interpretable features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KronSAE, a Kronecker-factorized sparse autoencoder with the mAND activation function, which reduces encoder computational cost and parameters while maintaining reconstruction fidelity and improving feature interpretability by reducing absorption.
papers.conclusion: KronSAE provides an efficient and interpretable alternative to standard sparse autoencoders, especially in resource-constrained settings, by synergizing Kronecker factorization and logical AND-style interactions to improve feature disentanglement.
papers.key_findings:
KronSAE achieves reconstruction quality comparable to baseline SAEs (TopK, Matryoshka, Switch) under iso-FLOPs constraints while using fewer parameters.
The architecture reduces feature absorption and yields more interpretable (monosemantic) latents, as measured by lower absorption scores and higher automated interpretability scores.
The mAND activation function and head-wise Cartesian decomposition are key design choices that enforce compositional structure and AND-like interactions, improving disentanglement.
KronSAE's pre-latents are often polysemantic, while post-latents are more specific, with retrieval mechanisms resembling logical AND operations.
The method introduces a trade-off between interpretability, efficiency, and reconstruction performance, controllable via hyperparameters (m, n, h).
papers.limitation: KronSAE introduces a trade-off between interpretability, efficiency, and reconstruction performance.
future_direction: Further exploration of the trade-offs and applications of KronSAE.
Developing more sophisticated techniques to identify the fine-grained structure of interactions between pre-latents.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have demonstrated significant promise in interpreting the hidden states of language models by decomposing them into interpretable latent directions. However, training and interpreting SAEs at scale remains challenging, especially when large dictionary sizes are used. While decoders can leverage sparse-aware kernels for efficiency, encoders still require computationally intensive linear operations with large output dimensions. To address this, we propose KronSAE, a novel architecture that factorizes the latent representation via Kronecker product decomposition, drastically reducing memory and computational overhead. Furthermore, we introduce mAND, a differentiable activation function approximating the binary AND operation, which improves interpretability and performance in our factorized framework.

papers.title: Structure-informed Language Models Are Protein Designers
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper demonstrates that language models are strong structure-based protein designers. We present LM-D esign , a generic approach to reprogramming sequence-based protein language models ( p LMs), that have learned massive sequential evolutionary knowledge from the universe of natural protein sequences, to acquire an immediate capability to design preferable protein sequences for given folds. We conduct a structural surgery on p LMs, where a lightweight structural adapter is implanted into p LMs and endows it with structural awareness. During inference, iterative refinement is performed to effectively optimize the generated protein sequences. Experiments show that LM-D esign improves the state-of-the-art results by a large margin, leading to 4% to 12% accuracy gains in sequence recovery ( e . g ., 55.65%/56.63% on CATH 4.2/4.3 single-chain benchmarks, and > 60% when designing protein complexes). We provide extensive and in-depth analyses, which verify that LM-D esign can (1) indeed leverage both structural and sequential knowledge to accurately handle structurally non-deterministic regions, (2) benefit from scaling data and model size, and (3) generalize to other proteins ( e . g ., antibodies and de novo proteins).

papers.title: Protein Language Model Supervised Precise and Efficient Protein Backbone Design Method
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Proteins are essential macromolecules that play crucial roles in nearly every type of biological function. Most of the protein functions are determined by their position topologies, indicating that new functional proteins might be generated by designing their tertiary structures initially. Over the past two decades, numerous energy-based and machine learning algorithms have been proposed for de novo protein design. However, optimizing these models to achieve a balanced performance among three critical aspects, namely sample fidelity, diversity, and generation speed, remains a challenging task on account of the constrained residue connections and hydrophobic interactions. Here we used the protein language model (pLM) as supervision to develop two complementary deep learning algorithms, Generative Protein Design by Language Model-Inpainting (GPDL-Inpainting) and GPDL-Hallucination, that can sufficiently represent and generate the protein structures and sequences. We compared the models with the state-of-the-art protein design models (RFdiffusion, RF Inpainting, and RF Halluciantion) and demonstrated that our methods can generate more designable structures with more diversity and higher computation efficiency. We also explored the possibility of the combination of hallucination and inpainting which might further improve the model efficiency and diversity. The source code of GPDL is available at https://github.com/sirius777coder/GPDL .

papers.title: Masked inverse folding with sequence transfer for protein representation learning
papers.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining on protein sequences has led to state-of-the art performance on protein function and fitness prediction. However, sequence-only methods ignore the rich information contained in experimental and predicted protein structures. Meanwhile, inverse folding methods reconstruct a protein's amino-acid sequence given its structure, but do not take advantage of sequences that do not have known structures. In this study, we train a masked inverse folding protein masked language model parameterized as a structured graph neural network. During pretraining, this model learns to reconstruct corrupted sequences conditioned on the backbone structure. We then show that using the outputs from a pretrained sequence-only protein masked language model as input to the inverse folding model further improves pretraining perplexity. We evaluate both of these models on downstream protein engineering tasks and analyze the effect of using information from experimental or predicted structures on performance.

papers.title: Inverse folding of protein complexes with a structure-informed language model enables unsupervised antibody evolution
papers.abstract: Large language models trained on sequence information alone are capable of learning high level principles of protein design. However, beyond sequence, the three-dimensional structures of proteins determine their specific function, activity, and evolvability. Here we show that a general protein language model augmented with protein structure backbone coordinates and trained on the inverse folding problem can guide evolution for diverse proteins without needing to explicitly model individual functional tasks. We demonstrate inverse folding to be an effective unsupervised, structure-based sequence optimization strategy that also generalizes to multimeric complexes by implicitly learning features of binding and amino acid epistasis. Using this approach, we screened ~30 variants of two therapeutic clinical antibodies used to treat SARS-CoV-2 infection and achieved up to 26-fold improvement in neutralization and 37-fold improvement in affinity against antibody-escaped viral variants-of-concern BQ.1.1 and XBB.1.5, respectively. In addition to substantial overall improvements in protein function, we find inverse folding performs with leading experimental success rates among other reported machine learning-guided directed evolution methods, without requiring any task-specific training data.

papers.title: ProteinReasoner: A Multi-Modal Protein Language Model with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Efficient Protein Design
papers.abstract: Abstract Protein language models (PLMs) have advanced the understanding and engineering of proteins by learning rich representations from large-scale sequence data. However, sequence-only models are limited in their ability to capture structural and evolutionary constraints essential for protein tasks. Although recent multi-modal PLMs integrate sequence and structure, they often fail to explicitly model the stepwise reasoning processes fundamental to protein science, particularly the evolutionary constraints and decision-making logic critical for protein design and optimization. Here, we introduce ProteinReasoner, a multi-modal protein language model that explicitly incorporates the “evolutionary profile” as the intermediate reasoning step between structure and sequence modalities within a chain-of-thought (CoT) framework. We demonstrated that ProteinReasoner achieved improved zero-shot performance in structure prediction, inverse protein folding, and fitness prediction tasks, consistently outperforming larger baselines including ESM3 and DPLM-2. Furthermore, we developed a novel In-context learning (ICL) paradigm for protein optimization that leverages ProteinReasoner’s reasoning capabilities to guide sequence generation based on prior experimental feedback. ProteinReasoner outperformed the conventional active learning paradigm in protein optimization tasks, achieving higher predictive accuracy and better generalization. ProteinReasoner offers a scalable, efficient, and generalizable framework for protein modeling and optimization, providing a practical path to accelerate protein engineering workflows and enhance mechanistic understanding of protein biology.

papers.title: Pretrained protein language models choose between sequence novelty and structural completeness
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have gained increasing acceptance in tasks ranging from variant effect prediction in disease to optimization and de novo design of proteins with improved stability, target-binding affinity, and catalytic performance. Despite encouraging performance in such applications, little is understood as far as the degree to which PLM-generated sequences - putative novel protein outputs - recapitulate the broad biophysical rules and diversity of sequence, structure, and function that defines natural protein-space, vital knowledge for boosting the design capacity of PLMs in ever-more-complex systems. Towards this end, we computationally profile and characterize the sequence and structure statistics and properties of hundreds of thousands of potential small proteins proposed through free unconstrained generation from architecturally distinct PLMs. We show that although these models exhibit a prodigious latent capacity to access novel amino-acid sequences, they struggle to approach the structural variation that exists on plain display in nature. Moreover, we uncover a stark tradeoff between prioritizing sequence novelty or structural breadth, exemplified by a "helical bundle trap" that dominates model output when aiming outside the comfortable bounds and evolutionary organization of natural sequences. These findings underscore a critical need for strategies that can rapidly guide PLMs into unlocking through generation the full richness of protein sequence, structure, and function that is consistent with governing biophysics but tantalizingly untapped as of yet in design contexts.

papers.title: Endowing Protein Language Models with Structural Knowledge
papers.abstract: Understanding the relationships between protein sequence, structure and function is a long-standing biological challenge with manifold implications from drug design to our understanding of evolution. Recently, protein language models have emerged as the preferred method for this challenge, thanks to their ability to harness large sequence databases. Yet, their reliance on expansive sequence data and parameter sets limits their flexibility and practicality in real-world scenarios. Concurrently, the recent surge in computationally predicted protein structures unlocks new opportunities in protein representation learning. While promising, the computational burden carried by such complex data still hinders widely-adopted practical applications. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel framework that enhances protein language models by integrating protein structural data. Drawing from recent advances in graph transformers, our approach refines the self-attention mechanisms of pretrained language transformers by integrating structural information with structure extractor modules. This refined model, termed Protein Structure Transformer (PST), is further pretrained on a small protein structure database, using the same masked language modeling objective as traditional protein language models. Empirical evaluations of PST demonstrate its superior parameter efficiency relative to protein language models, despite being pretrained on a dataset comprising only 542K structures. Notably, PST consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art foundation model for protein sequences, ESM-2, setting a new benchmark in protein function prediction. Our findings underscore the potential of integrating structural information into protein language models, paving the way for more effective and efficient protein modeling Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/PST.

papers.title: The promises of large language models for protein design and modeling
papers.abstract: The recent breakthroughs of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the context of natural language processing have opened the way to significant advances in protein research. Indeed, the relationships between human natural language and the "language of proteins" invite the application and adaptation of LLMs to protein modelling and design. Considering the impressive results of GPT-4 and other recently developed LLMs in processing, generating and translating human languages, we anticipate analogous results with the language of proteins. Indeed, protein language models have been already trained to accurately predict protein properties, generate novel functionally characterized proteins, achieving state-of-the-art results.
