papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are effective tools for interpreting audio-processing models, providing stable and interpretable features that have practical applications such as hallucination reduction and show alignment with human neural processing.
papers.key_findings:
Over 50% of SAE features remain consistent across random seeds.
SAE features capture general acoustic and semantic information as well as specific events like environmental noises and paralinguistic sounds.
Features disentangle concepts effectively, requiring removal of only 19–27% of features to erase a concept.
Feature steering reduces Whisper’s false speech detections by 70% with negligible WER increase.
SAE features are correlated with human EEG activity during speech perception, indicating alignment with human neural processing.
papers.limitation: The auto-interpretation method depends on empirically selected thresholds and is biased by the predominance of speech data in the test set, potentially obscuring rarer music or sound events, and is limited by the capabilities of the underlying audio captioning model.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are powerful tools for interpreting neural representations, yet their use in audio remains underexplored. We train SAEs across all encoder layers of Whisper and HuBERT, provide an extensive evaluation of their stability, interpretability, and show their practical utility. Over 50% of the features remain consistent across random seeds, and reconstruction quality is preserved. SAE features capture general acoustic and semantic information as well as specific events, including environmental noises and paralinguistic sounds (e.g. laughter, whispering) and disentangle them effectively, requiring removal of only 19-27% of features to erase a concept. Feature steering reduces Whisper's false speech detections by 70% with negligible WER increase, demonstrating real-world applicability. Finally, we find SAE features correlated with human EEG activity during speech perception, indicating alignment with human neural processing. The code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/audiosae/audiosae_demo.

papers.title: TopK Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we build a language model architecture that enjoys the interpretability of sparse autoencoders without suffering the drawbacks of post-hoc training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TopK LMs, a transformer-based language model architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function to achieve inherent, SAE-like interpretability without requiring post-hoc training, while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: TopK LMs represent a significant advance toward trustworthy AI systems by making interpretability a built-in feature, demonstrating that performance and interpretability need not be competing objectives.
papers.key_findings:
TopK LMs achieve competitive language modeling and downstream task performance compared to dense baselines, with only a moderate increase in model size.
Neurons in TopK LMs exhibit higher concept specialization, as measured by lower token and semantic entropy, making them more interpretable.
Single-neuron interventions (activation patching) can causally steer the model's text generation towards specific concepts.
The formation and specialization of individual neurons can be traced continuously across training checkpoints and model layers.
Sparsity annealing during training improves convergence and model performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models up to ~1B parameters; effectiveness on significantly larger models remains an open question.
Evaluation focused on language modeling and standard reasoning benchmarks, leaving performance on specialized downstream tasks unclear.
Long-context modeling capabilities and the interaction between TopK sparsity and attention over long sequences were not examined.
The approach is currently limited to text-only models; extending to multimodal architectures requires future research.
Specific societal applications that could benefit from the model's interpretability were not explored.
future_direction: Scaling the TopK LM approach to significantly larger models (tens or hundreds of billions of parameters).
Extending TopK activation to multimodal architectures combining text with images, audio, or other modalities.
Investigating how TopK LMs can address concrete challenges in model alignment, fairness assessment, safety evaluation, and trustworthy AI deployment.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for analyzing and interpreting the activation space of transformer-based language models (LMs). However, SAEs suffer several shortcomings that diminish their utility and internal validity. Since SAEs are trained post-hoc, it is unclear if the failure to discover a particular concept is a failure on the SAE's side or due to the underlying LM not representing this concept. This problem is exacerbated by training conditions and architecture choices affecting which features an SAE learns. When tracing how LMs learn concepts during training, the lack of feature stability also makes it difficult to compare SAEs features across different checkpoints. To address these limitations, we introduce a modification to the transformer architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function at chosen layers, making the model's hidden states equivalent to the latent features of a TopK SAE. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc training while providing interpretability comparable to SAEs. The resulting TopK LMs offer a favorable trade-off between model size, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Despite this simple architectural change, TopK LMs maintain their original capabilities while providing robust interpretability benefits. Our experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations learned by TopK LMs enable successful steering through targeted neuron interventions and facilitate detailed analysis of neuron formation processes across checkpoints and layers. These features make TopK LMs stable and reliable tools for understanding how language models learn and represent concepts, which we believe will significantly advance future research on model interpretability and controllability.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the structure of SAE error (dark matter)? Can SAE error be predicted from activations? How do the linearly predictable and nonlinearly predictable components differ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that SAE error (dark matter) is largely linearly predictable from model activations, and that the nonlinear component is qualitatively different, containing fewer not-yet-learned features and being harder to learn.
papers.conclusion: The fact that SAE error can be predicted and analyzed is surprising, indicating SAE errors are worthy of analysis. The presence of constant nonlinear error at fixed sparsity suggests scaling SAEs may not be the only way to explain more of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAE error norms and vectors can be linearly predicted from activations with high accuracy (R2 between 70-95% for norms, 15-72% for vectors).
The scaling behavior of SAE error norms is predictable across different SAE sizes; larger SAEs struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs.
The nonlinear component of SAE error contains fewer not-yet-learned features, is harder to learn SAEs for, and contributes proportionally to cross entropy loss.
Inference time gradient pursuit reduces total FVU by 3-5% but leaves nonlinear error mostly unchanged.
Linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs can reduce nonlinear error and total SAE error.
future_direction: Explore alternative penalties besides sparsity or new ways to learn better dictionaries.
Incorporate low-rank dense side channels in SAE architecture.
Use small-scale trials to forecast SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising technique for decomposing language model activations into interpretable linear features. However, current SAEs fall short of completely explaining model performance, resulting in "dark matter": unexplained variance in activations. This work investigates dark matter as an object of study in its own right. Surprisingly, we find that much of SAE dark matter -- about half of the error vector itself and >90% of its norm -- can be linearly predicted from the initial activation vector. Additionally, we find that the scaling behavior of SAE error norms at a per token level is remarkably predictable: larger SAEs mostly struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs. We build on the linear representation hypothesis to propose models of activations that might lead to these observations. These insights imply that the part of the SAE error vector that cannot be linearly predicted ("nonlinear" error) might be fundamentally different from the linearly predictable component. To validate this hypothesis, we empirically analyze nonlinear SAE error and show that 1) it contains fewer not yet learned features, 2) SAEs trained on it are quantitatively worse, and 3) it is responsible for a proportional amount of the downstream increase in cross entropy loss when SAE activations are inserted into the model. Finally, we examine two methods to reduce nonlinear SAE error: inference time gradient pursuit, which leads to a very slight decrease in nonlinear error, and linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs, which leads to a larger reduction.

papers.title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How does the L0 hyperparameter (average number of active features per token) in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) affect the quality of learned features, and how can the correct L0 be determined?
papers.core_contribution: The L0 hyperparameter in Sparse Autoencoders must be set correctly to learn monosemantic features; if L0 is too low or too high, the SAE mixes correlated features, and the paper provides a proxy metric (decoder pairwise cosine similarity) to guide L0 selection.
papers.conclusion: The L0 hyperparameter must be set correctly for SAEs to learn correct, monosemantic features, and most existing SAEs likely have an L0 that is too low.
papers.key_findings:
If L0 is set too low, SAEs mix positively correlated features to improve reconstruction, leading to polysemantic latents.
If L0 is set too high, SAEs find degenerate solutions that also mix features.
Commonly used sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots are not a sound evaluation method, as they can favor incorrect SAEs that mix features over a ground-truth SAE.
A proxy metric, decoder pairwise cosine similarity (c_dec), is minimized when the SAE L0 matches the true underlying L0 of the data distribution.
Most commonly used open-source SAEs have an L0 that is too low.
papers.limitation:
The investigation is limited to features satisfying the linear representation hypothesis and does not consider non-linear underlying features.
The study only investigated a few layers of popular LLMs due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Investigate how SAEs react if the underlying features are non-linear.
Explore the impact of different correlation structures (e.g., unbalanced correlations) on SAEs.
Extend the analysis to more layers of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) extract features from LLM internal activations, meant to correspond to interpretable concepts. A core SAE training hyperparameter is L0: how many SAE features should fire per token on average. Existing work compares SAE algorithms using sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots, implying L0 is a free parameter with no single correct value aside from its effect on reconstruction. In this work we study the effect of L0 on SAEs, and show that if L0 is not set correctly, the SAE fails to disentangle the underlying features of the LLM. If L0 is too low, the SAE will mix correlated features to improve reconstruction. If L0 is too high, the SAE finds degenerate solutions that also mix features. Further, we present a proxy metric that can help guide the search for the correct L0 for an SAE on a given training distribution. We show that our method finds the correct L0 in toy models and coincides with peak sparse probing performance in LLM SAEs. We find that most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low. Our work shows that L0 must be set correctly to train SAEs with correct features.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Safe-SAIL: Towards a Fine-grained Safety Landscape of Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoder Interpretation Framework
papers.research_question: Under what circumstances do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) derive the most fine-grained latent features for safety—a low-frequency concept domain? How can we efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduce the cost of feature explanation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features in safety-critical domains, which includes a pre-explanation evaluation metric to efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduces interpretation cost by 55% via segment-level simulation.
papers.conclusion: Safe-SAIL is a novel SAE interpretation framework that generates more granular safety feature explanations and reduces explanation costs by half, offering an internal perspective and methodology to address problems in LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Safe-SAIL reduces the cost of feature explanation by 55% through a segment-level simulation strategy while maintaining high correlation with token-level results.
The framework enables the identification of optimal SAE sparsity levels for safety domain-specific interpretability, which differs from the sparsity for minimal feature interference.
A comprehensive suite of SAEs trained on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct is released, with human-readable explanations for 1,758 safety-related features across pornography, politics, violence, and terror domains.
Empirical analyses reveal how LLMs encode specific real-world risk entities (e.g., pornographic websites) and safety-critical concepts across model layers.
The work provides insights into model cognition and reasoning trajectories, particularly highlighting failure modes in low-resource languages where relevant safety features are not activated.
papers.limitation:
The safety feature database covers only four major risk domains; extending it to emerging safety concerns would broaden applicability.
Explanation quality depends on the explainer model's capabilities, which may vary across languages and technical domains.
Segment-level simulation offers efficiency gains but approximates token-level dynamics; applications requiring maximal granularity may benefit from hybrid approaches.
Evaluation metrics rely on empirically validated thresholds that could benefit from automated domain-adaptive tuning.
Analyses primarily identify strong correlational patterns; establishing causal mechanisms through controlled interventions remains an important next step.
future_direction: Extending the safety feature database to emerging safety concerns such as privacy leakage, model self-replication, or deceptive alignment.
Improving explanation quality across languages and technical domains.
Developing hybrid simulation approaches for applications requiring maximal granularity.
Automated domain-adaptive tuning for evaluation metrics.
Systematic causal validation of the broader feature set through controlled interventions.
papers.abstract: Increasing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications raises significant safety concerns. Most existing safety research focuses on evaluating LLM outputs or specific safety tasks, limiting their ability to address broader, undefined risks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) facilitate interpretability research to clarify model behavior by explaining single-meaning atomic features decomposed from entangled signals. jHowever, prior applications on SAEs do not interpret features with fine-grained safety-related concepts, thus inadequately addressing safety-critical behaviors, such as generating toxic responses and violating safety regulations. For rigorous safety analysis, we must extract a rich and diverse set of safety-relevant features that effectively capture these high-risk behaviors, yet face two challenges: identifying SAEs with the greatest potential for generating safety concept-specific neurons, and the prohibitively high cost of detailed feature explanation. In this paper, we propose Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features within LLMs to advance mechanistic understanding in safety domains. Our approach systematically identifies SAE with best concept-specific interpretability, explains safety-related neurons, and introduces efficient strategies to scale up the interpretation process. We will release a comprehensive toolkit including SAE checkpoints and human-readable neuron explanations, which supports empirical analysis of safety risks to promote research on LLM safety.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we train sparse autoencoders to learn hierarchical features and avoid pathologies like feature absorption and splitting when scaling dictionary size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders, a hierarchical variant that trains multiple nested dictionaries simultaneously to learn features at different levels of abstraction, reducing feature absorption and splitting.
papers.conclusion: Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical interpretability tasks, enabling training of arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Matryoshka SAEs significantly reduce feature absorption and splitting compared to standard SAEs.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve more disentangled latent representations and better performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks.
Matryoshka SAEs maintain or improve downstream task performance with increasing dictionary size, unlike standard SAEs which often degrade.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit a small trade-off in reconstruction fidelity but learn more meaningful features that result in comparable downstream model loss.
The hierarchical structure forces early latents to capture general concepts and later latents to specialize, preserving interpretable features at multiple scales.
papers.limitation:
Slightly reduced reconstruction performance compared to standard SAEs.
Increased training time due to multiple nested reconstruction objectives.
Reliance on quantitative metrics that may not fully capture human-relevant interpretability.
future_direction: Investigate the human interpretability of Matryoshka SAE latents.
Explore the applicability of Matryoshka SAEs to practical interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting neural networks by extracting the concepts represented in their activations. However, choosing the size of the SAE dictionary (i.e. number of learned concepts) creates a tension: as dictionary size increases to capture more relevant concepts, sparsity incentivizes features to be split or absorbed into more specific features, leaving high-level features missing or warped. We introduce Matryoshka SAEs, a novel variant that addresses these issues by simultaneously training multiple nested dictionaries of increasing size, forcing the smaller dictionaries to independently reconstruct the inputs without using the larger dictionaries. This organizes features hierarchically - the smaller dictionaries learn general concepts, while the larger dictionaries learn more specific concepts, without incentive to absorb the high-level features. We train Matryoshka SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and TinyStories and find superior performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks, more disentangled concept representations, and reduced feature absorption. While there is a minor tradeoff with reconstruction performance, we believe Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical tasks, as they enable training arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.

papers.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do various representation-based steering methods compare to prompting and finetuning in terms of concept detection and model steering for language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AXBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating steering and concept detection methods, and finds that prompting outperforms representation-based methods for steering, while difference-in-means and probes are best for detection, with the novel ReFT-r1 method being competitive on both tasks.
papers.conclusion: Representation steering methods largely lag behind prompting and finetuning, but ReFT-r1 shows that steering can be improved with comprehensive benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting is the best method for model steering, outperforming all representation-based methods.
Difference-in-means, linear probes, and ReFT-r1 perform best for concept detection with no significant difference between them.
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are not competitive compared to other methods on both steering and detection.
ReFT-r1, a novel weakly-supervised method, is competitive on both steering and detection tasks while offering interpretability advantages.
The AXBENCH benchmark enables comprehensive evaluation and comparison of steering methods.
papers.limitation: Hyperparameter tuning might underestimate steering performance due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Extend AXBENCH to arbitrary concept descriptions and add new evaluation tasks as better feature-labelling techniques and steering approaches emerge.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

papers.title: On the transferability of Sparse Autoencoders for interpreting compressed models
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) trained on uncompressed models be effectively transferred to interpret compressed (pruned) models, and is pruning the original SAE itself a viable alternative to training a new SAE on the pruned model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs pretrained on uncompressed models can be transferred to pruned models with minimal performance loss, and pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, offering a computationally efficient alternative.
papers.conclusion: Retraining SAEs for each compressed model variant may be unnecessary; pruning the pretrained SAE offers a practical and computationally efficient alternative for post-hoc interpretability analysis of compressed models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model with only slight performance degradation compared to SAEs trained on the compressed model.
Pruning a pretrained SAE (e.g., to 25% sparsity) yields performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, eliminating the need for costly retraining.
The transferability and pruning effectiveness hold across different model architectures (GPT-2 and Gemma-2-2B) and across various interpretability metrics (reconstruction, feature absorption, SCR, TPP, RAVEL).
future_direction: Explore the generalization of these findings to quantized and low-rank compressed models.
Further investigate the role of pruning as an implicit regularizer in interpretability systems.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs face inference efficiency challenges due to their scale. To address this, many compression methods have been proposed, such as pruning and quantization. However, the effect of compression on a model's interpretability remains elusive. While several model interpretation approaches exist, such as circuit discovery, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have proven particularly effective in decomposing a model's activation space into its feature basis. In this work, we explore the differences in SAEs for the original and compressed models. We find that SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model albeit with slight performance degradation compared to the trained SAE on the compressed model. Furthermore, simply pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model. This finding enables us to mitigate the extensive training costs of SAEs.

papers.title: Dense SAE Latents Are Features, Not Bugs
papers.research_question: Are dense latents in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) undesirable training artifacts or do they reflect meaningful model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Dense SAE latents are not training artifacts but reflect meaningful, functional representations in the language model's residual stream, serving roles such as position tracking, context binding, and entropy regulation.
papers.conclusion: Dense SAE latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the dense-latent subspace in the residual stream prevents new dense latents from being learned in retrained SAEs, indicating dense features are intrinsic to the residual space.
Dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream.
A taxonomy of dense latents identifies classes including position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, alphabet (letter-specific output), part-of-speech, and PCA reconstruction.
The function of dense latents shifts across layers: from structural (e.g., position) in early layers, to semantic (e.g., context binding) in middle layers, to output-oriented (e.g., alphabet) in late layers.
Nullspace-aligned dense latents are causally involved in entropy regulation via interaction with RMSNorm scaling.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a few models (Gemma 2 2B, GPT-2, LLaMA 3.2) and SAE architectures (JumpReLU, TopK).
future_direction: Explore the circuits involving dense subspaces, particularly context-binding latents.
Investigate whether dense latents are a general phenomenon across more models and SAE variants.
Challenge the assumption of globally monosemantic directions and further study context-dependent feature binding.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to extract interpretable features from language models by enforcing a sparsity constraint. Ideally, training an SAE would yield latents that are both sparse and semantically meaningful. However, many SAE latents activate frequently (i.e., are \emph{dense}), raising concerns that they may be undesirable artifacts of the training procedure. In this work, we systematically investigate the geometry, function, and origin of dense latents and show that they are not only persistent but often reflect meaningful model representations. We first demonstrate that dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream, and that ablating their subspace suppresses the emergence of new dense features in retrained SAEs -- suggesting that high density features are an intrinsic property of the residual space. We then introduce a taxonomy of dense latents, identifying classes tied to position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, letter-specific output signals, part-of-speech, and principal component reconstruction. Finally, we analyze how these features evolve across layers, revealing a shift from structural features in early layers, to semantic features in mid layers, and finally to output-oriented signals in the last layers of the model. Our findings indicate that dense latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to reduce biases like shrinkage and achieve better sparsity and reconstruction fidelity in language model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gated SAEs that decouple feature detection and magnitude estimation, solving shrinkage and providing Pareto improvements in sparsity and reconstruction fidelity over baseline SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Gated SAEs are a promising improvement for sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability, offering better performance and reduced biases.
papers.key_findings:
Gated SAEs achieve better reconstruction fidelity at any given level of sparsity compared to baseline SAEs.
Gated SAEs effectively address the shrinkage problem, with reconstructions being unbiased.
Gated SAE features are similarly interpretable to baseline SAE features based on human evaluation.
Ablation studies show that freezing the decoder in the auxiliary task and weight tying are important for performance.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are an effective technique for unsupervised discovery of interpretable features in language models' (LMs) activations, by finding sparse, linear reconstructions of LM activations. We introduce the Gated Sparse Autoencoder (Gated SAE), which achieves a Pareto improvement over training with prevailing methods. In SAEs, the L1 penalty used to encourage sparsity introduces many undesirable biases, such as shrinkage -- systematic underestimation of feature activations. The key insight of Gated SAEs is to separate the functionality of (a) determining which directions to use and (b) estimating the magnitudes of those directions: this enables us to apply the L1 penalty only to the former, limiting the scope of undesirable side effects. Through training SAEs on LMs of up to 7B parameters we find that, in typical hyper-parameter ranges, Gated SAEs solve shrinkage, are similarly interpretable, and require half as many firing features to achieve comparable reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: Visual Exploration of Feature Relationships in Sparse Autoencoders with Curated Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we enable effective, focused exploration of the relationships between sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and human-interpretable concepts in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a focused exploration framework and an interactive visualization system (SAE Semantic Explorer) that integrates topology-based visual encodings with dimensionality reduction to enable targeted analysis of relationships between SAE features and curated concepts.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization framework provides a scalable and interpretable means of exploring how user-defined concepts relate to the structured knowledge encoded in SAEs across layers, facilitating deeper insight into model organization.
papers.key_findings:
The framework reveals that concept relationships evolve across model layers, with early layers showing dense clustering, middle layers showing separation and specialization, and deeper layers showing more integrated structures.
The ball mapper view provides a complementary perspective to UMAP, preserving local neighborhood relationships and revealing structural distortions introduced by dimensionality reduction.
The tool enables the discovery of semantic boundaries and transitions between related concepts, such as tracing a path from 'Computer Science' to 'Mathematics' in the feature space.
papers.limitation: The reliability of identified features depends heavily on the quality of their automatically generated explanations (auto-interpretability).
future_direction: Enhance the UMAP visualization by integrating scalable and annotated visualization toolkits.
Leverage LLMs to automatically generate richer, context-aware explanations for mapper nodes.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for uncovering interpretable features in large language models (LLMs) through the sparse directions they learn. However, the sheer number of extracted directions makes comprehensive exploration intractable. While conventional embedding techniques such as UMAP can reveal global structure, they suffer from limitations including high-dimensional compression artifacts, overplotting, and misleading neighborhood distortions. In this work, we propose a focused exploration framework that prioritizes curated concepts and their corresponding SAE features over attempts to visualize all available features simultaneously. We present an interactive visualization system that combines topology-based visual encoding with dimensionality reduction to faithfully represent both local and global relationships among selected features. This hybrid approach enables users to investigate SAE behavior through targeted, interpretable subsets, facilitating deeper and more nuanced analysis of concept representation in latent space.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: Do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) improve performance on LLM activation probing tasks in challenging regimes such as data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift?
papers.core_contribution: SAE probes do not consistently outperform baseline probing methods across various challenging regimes, and baseline methods can achieve similar interpretability insights.
papers.conclusion: Current SAEs do not offer a consistent advantage for probing tasks, highlighting the need for rigorous evaluation of interpretability methods with strong baselines.
papers.key_findings:
SAE probes underperform baseline logistic regression on average across datasets in standard conditions.
SAE probes do not provide a consistent advantage in data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift regimes.
Baseline methods can provide similar interpretability insights as SAE probes, such as detecting dataset issues.
Pruning SAE latents based on autointerp descriptions can slightly improve out-of-distribution generalization but not enough to match the performance drop.
SAE latents sometimes fail to generalize out-of-distribution, e.g., a latent for 'living room' only fires on English phrases.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to probing tasks and may not generalize to other tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for interpreting concepts represented in large language model (LLM) activations. However, there is a lack of evidence regarding the validity of their interpretations due to the lack of a ground truth for the concepts used by an LLM, and a growing number of works have presented problems with current SAEs. One alternative source of evidence would be demonstrating that SAEs improve performance on downstream tasks beyond existing baselines. We test this by applying SAEs to the real-world task of LLM activation probing in four regimes: data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift. Due to the difficulty of detecting concepts in these challenging settings, we hypothesize that SAEs' basis of interpretable, concept-level latents should provide a useful inductive bias. However, although SAEs occasionally perform better than baselines on individual datasets, we are unable to design ensemble methods combining SAEs with baselines that consistently outperform ensemble methods solely using baselines. Additionally, although SAEs initially appear promising for identifying spurious correlations, detecting poor dataset quality, and training multi-token probes, we are able to achieve similar results with simple non-SAE baselines as well. Though we cannot discount SAEs' utility on other tasks, our findings highlight the shortcomings of current SAEs and the need to rigorously evaluate interpretability methods on downstream tasks with strong baselines.

papers.title: CE-Bench: Towards a Reliable Contrastive Evaluation Benchmark of Interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we create a reliable, LLM-free benchmark to evaluate the interpretability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CE-Bench, a fully LLM-free, contrastive evaluation benchmark for sparse autoencoders that measures interpretability via activation differences across curated story pairs, achieving strong alignment with existing LLM-assisted benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CE-Bench is a stable, deterministic, and reproducible framework for evaluating sparse autoencoder interpretability without relying on external LLMs, closely aligning with existing benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
CE-Bench achieves over 70% Spearman correlation with SAEBench rankings, providing a reliable LLM-free alternative.
Top-k and p-anneal SAE architectures consistently yield the highest interpretability scores.
Wider latent spaces (e.g., 65k dimensions) lead to higher interpretability scores, suggesting better feature disentanglement.
Interpretability scores are largely invariant to the type of transformer sub-layer (attention, MLP, residual) being probed.
Middle transformer layers (e.g., layers 10 and 15) provide the clearest semantic representations and highest interpretability scores.
papers.limitation:
The dataset of 5000 contrastive story pairs was generated using GPT-4, which may bias the evaluation toward models that capture GPT-4's stylistic and semantic regularities.
The dataset is limited in domain coverage, focusing mainly on synthetic narrative text, so its generalizability to varied or domain-specific contexts is uncertain.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach for uncovering interpretable features in large language models (LLMs). While several automated evaluation methods exist for SAEs, most rely on external LLMs. In this work, we introduce CE-Bench, a novel and lightweight contrastive evaluation benchmark for sparse autoencoders, built on a curated dataset of contrastive story pairs. We conduct comprehensive evaluation studies to validate the effectiveness of our approach. Our results show that CE-Bench reliably measures the interpretability of sparse autoencoders and aligns well with existing benchmarks without requiring an external LLM judge, achieving over 70% Spearman correlation with results in SAEBench. The official implementation and evaluation dataset are open-sourced and publicly available.

papers.title: Features that Make a Difference: Leveraging Gradients for Improved Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be improved to learn features that are more causally relevant to model outputs by incorporating gradient information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gradient SAEs (g-SAEs), which modify the TopK activation function in sparse autoencoders to incorporate gradient information, resulting in latents that are more causally relevant and better for steering model outputs without sacrificing interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating gradient information into SAEs improves their ability to capture causally relevant features and enhances steerability without compromising interpretability, advancing dictionary learning towards accounting for both representational and causal aspects of model features.
papers.key_findings:
g-SAEs produce reconstructions that are more faithful to original network performance for a given sparsity level.
g-SAEs learn latents that are more effective at steering models in arbitrary contexts, increasing the probability of associated tokens more strongly and specifically.
g-SAEs have fewer permanently inactive ('dead') latents compared to other SAE architectures.
g-SAEs show improved performance (lower loss added) across different model sizes (GPT-2 small to xl).
g-SAEs do not sacrifice interpretability, as human evaluators rate them similarly to standard TopK SAEs.
papers.limitation:
Activation plateaus: models may be robust to small perturbations, so gradients might not capture sensitivity to larger perturbations.
Computational complexity: g-SAEs require backpropagation, though in practice it was not a bottleneck.
Evaluations: need for more thorough evaluations and understanding of how token-level steerability translates to higher levels of abstraction.
future_direction: Investigating how to incorporate higher-order derivative information to address activation plateaus.
Developing more comprehensive evaluation frameworks for SAEs.
Studying how increased steerability on the token level translates to higher levels of abstraction.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach for extracting neural network features by learning a sparse and overcomplete decomposition of the network's internal activations.However, SAEs are traditionally trained considering only activation values and not the effect those activations have on downstream computations.This limits the information available to learn features, and biases the autoencoder towards neglecting features which are represented with small activation values but strongly influence model outputs.To address this, we introduce Gradient SAEs (g-SAEs), which modify the k-sparse autoencoder architecture by augmenting the TopK activation function to rely on the gradients of the input activation when selecting the k elements.For a given sparsity level, g-SAEs produce reconstructions that are more faithful to original network performance when propagated through the network.Additionally, we find evidence that g-SAEs learn latents that are on average more effective at steering models in arbitrary contexts.By considering the downstream effects of activations, our approach leverages the dual nature of neural network features as both representations, retrospectively, and actions, prospectively.While previous methods have approached the problem of feature discovery primarily focused on the former aspect, g-SAEs represent a step towards accounting for the latter as well.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders: From Shallow Design to Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the limitations of shallow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in extracting correlated features due to an implicit quasi-orthogonality assumption, and proposes an iterative SAE based on Matching Pursuit (MP-SAE) to overcome these limitations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, an iterative sparse autoencoder that unrolls Matching Pursuit, which improves expressivity, learns hierarchical features, and overcomes the coherence limitations of shallow SAEs by enabling residual-guided extraction of correlated features.
papers.conclusion: MP-SAE improves expressivity, learns hierarchical features, and overcomes the coherence limitations of shallow SAEs, providing a foundation for building more interpretable sparse autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
MP-SAE is more expressive than shallow SAEs across varying sparsity levels and dictionary sizes.
MP-SAE learns a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine feature structure, with early atoms capturing digit prototypes and later atoms refining pen strokes.
MP-SAE learns a globally coherent dictionary but selects more incoherent subsets of atoms during inference, unlike shallow SAEs where dictionary and selected atom coherence align.
MP-SAE guarantees monotonic improvement in reconstruction as more atoms are selected, a property not shared by other SAEs.
Shallow SAEs (ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK, BatchTopK) exhibit distinct structural biases in their learned dictionaries, such as ReLU learning full-digit atoms and others learning pen-stroke patterns.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently become central tools for interpretability, leveraging dictionary learning principles to extract sparse, interpretable features from neural representations whose underlying structure is typically unknown. This paper evaluates SAEs in a controlled setting using MNIST, which reveals that current shallow architectures implicitly rely on a quasi-orthogonality assumption that limits the ability to extract correlated features. To move beyond this, we compare them with an iterative SAE that unrolls Matching Pursuit (MP-SAE), enabling the residual-guided extraction of correlated features that arise in hierarchical settings such as handwritten digit generation while guaranteeing monotonic improvement of the reconstruction as more atoms are selected.

papers.title: Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the reconstruction fidelity of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at a given sparsity level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces JumpReLU SAEs, a simple modification of ReLU SAEs that achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level and is similarly interpretable to other SAE methods.
papers.conclusion: JumpReLU SAEs are a mild improvement over prevailing SAE training methodologies, offering better or equal reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity, similar interpretability, and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
JumpReLU SAEs consistently provide more faithful reconstructions than Gated SAEs and at least as good as, and often slightly better than, TopK SAEs at a given sparsity level.
JumpReLU SAEs have few dead features without the need for resampling during training.
JumpReLU SAEs have a similar proportion of very high frequency features (active on >10% of tokens) as TopK SAEs, which is higher than Gated SAEs.
Manual and automated interpretability studies show that JumpReLU SAE features are similarly interpretable to Gated and TopK SAE features.
JumpReLU SAEs are efficient to train, requiring no auxiliary loss terms and having an elementwise activation function (unlike TopK).
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are conducted on a single model (Gemma 2 9B), raising uncertainty about transfer to other models.
The science of principled evaluations of SAE performance is still in its infancy; it is unclear how well current metrics correlate with downstream utility.
JumpReLU SAEs tend to have relatively more very high frequency features than Gated SAEs.
JumpReLU SAEs introduce new hyperparameters (initial threshold and bandwidth) that require selection.
future_direction: Evaluate SAEs on a broader selection of metrics that more directly correspond to the value SAEs add by aiding or enabling downstream tasks, such as circuit analysis or model control.
Further tweak the loss function used to train JumpReLU SAEs to directly tackle the phenomenon of high frequency features.
Develop more principled ways to choose hyperparameters, such as the bandwidth parameter, possibly borrowing from kernel density estimation literature.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising unsupervised approach for identifying causally relevant and interpretable linear features in a language model's (LM) activations. To be useful for downstream tasks, SAEs need to decompose LM activations faithfully; yet to be interpretable the decomposition must be sparse -- two objectives that are in tension. In this paper, we introduce JumpReLU SAEs, which achieve state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level on Gemma 2 9B activations, compared to other recent advances such as Gated and TopK SAEs. We also show that this improvement does not come at the cost of interpretability through manual and automated interpretability studies. JumpReLU SAEs are a simple modification of vanilla (ReLU) SAEs -- where we replace the ReLU with a discontinuous JumpReLU activation function -- and are similarly efficient to train and run. By utilising straight-through-estimators (STEs) in a principled manner, we show how it is possible to train JumpReLU SAEs effectively despite the discontinuous JumpReLU function introduced in the SAE's forward pass. Similarly, we use STEs to directly train L0 to be sparse, instead of training on proxies such as L1, avoiding problems like shrinkage.

papers.title: Training Superior Sparse Autoencoders for Instruct Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on instruct models, given that existing methods designed for base models result in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability?
